title: Jina AI (@JinaAI_) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Convert your embeddings to spherical coordinates before compression - this trick cuts embedding storage from 240 GB to 160 GB, and 25% better than the best lossless baseline. Reconstruction is near-lossless as the error stays below float32 machine epsilon - so retrieval quality is preserved perfectly. Works across text, image, and multi-vector embeddings. No training, no codebooks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_XWrOGbAAIpOdn.jpg
────────
[2/3] Here's why it works: embeddings lie on a hypersphere, so d-1 angles can replace d Cartesian coordinates. In high dimensions, those angles concentrate around pi/2, causing IEEE 754 exponents to collapse to a single value. This makes the byte stream highly compressible.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_XUwxYWgAAcfIz.jpg
────────
[3/3] Here's an visualization for jina-embeddings-v4 vectors. This concentration collapses exponents to a single dominant value of 127, reducing exponent entropy from 2.6 to 0.03 bits/byte for jina-v4. But bxponent compression alone would yield only 1.1x compression. The additional gain comes from the high-order mantissa byte: when angles cluster around π/2 ≈1.5708, the IEEE
754 mantissa bits encoding the fractional part also become predictable. Empirically, the high-order
mantissa byte entropy drops from 8.0 to 4.5 bits. Together, exponent and mantissa concentration yield the observed 1.5x compression
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_XVS82bQAAEnwJ.jpg

[2/3] Text embeddings are widely assumed to be safe, irreversible representations. We show we can reconstruct the original text using conditional masked diffusion.
Existing inversions (Vec2Text, ALGEN, Zero2Text) generate tokens autoregressively and require iterative re-embedding through the target encoder. We take a different approach: embedding inversion as conditional masked diffusion. Starting from a fully masked sequence, a denoising model reveals tokens at all positions in parallel, conditioned on the target embedding via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN-Zero). Each denoising step refines all positions simultaneously using global context, without ever re-embedding the current hypothesis.

title: Julian Killingback (@Julian_a42f9a) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] I’m excited to share our new work “Scaling Laws for Embedding Dimension in Information Retrieval” which explores the scaling behavior of dense retrieval models at different embedding dimensions.
────────
[2/7] Dense retrieval has become the dominant approach for neural search, but often the embedding dimension, which plays a crucial role in both the index size and information capacity, is treated as a fixed hyperparameter.
────────
[3/7] We systematically evaluated how scaling embedding dimension impacts retrieval performance and produce scaling laws which accurately predict performance, including a joint scaling law which considers both embedding dimension and model size.
────────
[4/7] We find that the scaling behavior follows a power law: performance tends to degrade significantly at small embedding dimensions, while the returns start to diminish as embeddings become larger.
────────
[5/7] We use our derived scaling laws to find the optimal model size and embedding dimension for a fixed inference FLOPs budget. We find that scaling both embedding dimension and model size is optimal.
────────
[6/7] For sub-linear search techniques, like approximate nearest neighbor search, we find that the optimal embedding dimension increases substantially in response to reduction in documents to score.
────────
[7/7] Our work provides the first systematic evaluation of the impact of embedding dimension and model scale, offering empirical results to complement prior theoretical work.
Check it out on Arxiv:

────────
[2/3] By substituting raw text with shorter late-interaction document representations, we achieve up to 10x compression while maintaining generation quality. This approach requires no additional storage space beyond what a standard late-interaction retriever already uses.
────────
[3/3] This is achieved by training a single decoder language model to function as a context compressor, embedder, and generator. Using a shared representation for both retrieval and the compressed context enables the space-saving unified representation.
clean_summary:
Late-interaction retrieval models are widely used for their strong performance, but their representations can be utilized beyond just retrieval. A new paper demonstrates that these representations can effectively replace raw document text in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tasks.

By substituting raw text with shorter late-interaction document representations, the approach achieves up to 10x compression while maintaining generation quality, requiring no additional storage space beyond what a standard late-interaction retriever already uses.

This is accomplished by training a single decoder language model to function as a context compressor, embedder, and generator. Using a shared representation for both retrieval and the compressed context enables the space-saving unified representation.

🔍🪡To find the needle, you better index every straw of the haystack.
Today, LightOn is launching LightOn NextPlaid: a CPU-optimized multi-vector database that indexes at the token level. By representing documents as sets of vectors, one per token, we preserve the distinct concepts and precise details that other search engines average away.
Why NextPlaid is the missing layer for your RAG stack:
🎯Precision Matching: Retrieval matches at the token level, surfacing the exact passage that answers your question rather than just a document that vaguely relates.
📉Frugal Inference: High-signal context reduces the amount of noise sent to your LLM, allowing it to answer with fewer, more accurate tokens.
🚀Seamless Integration: NextPlaid runs alongside your existing vector database. You can add multi-vector retrieval to your established RAG pipeline without ripping anything out.
⚙️Production Ready: Built in Rust and optimized for CPUs, it supports incremental index updates and concurrent reads/writes—capabilities missing from standard implementations.
NextPlaid represents the "Blanc" milestone in our Bleu/Blanc/Rouge roadmap for enterprise document intelligence. It follows the "Bleu" release, LightOnOCR-2, a SOTA 1B OCR model which converts complex documents into clean, usable text.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
The "RAG is dead" debate often misses the fact that the 10M context window models that are "burying RAG" are probably just doing some form of RAG over their own context. Very unlikely you get any sort of Needle In a Haystack performance by compressing in a fixed sized memory buffer, and the inference cost of quadratic attention is prohibitive at this length.
So you're still "indexing" by constructing a KV cache (+tricks) during the prefill which you store in a data structure, and "retrieving" relevant context in the form of KV caches to feed the model.
Lots of tricks are possible: "landmark attention" learns a representation of context chunks which are matched to queries with cosine distance (sounds familiar), DeepSeek v3.2 stores a compressed representation of the keys to be quickly matched to queries and construct a top k of KVs to "really" feed to the model. Those are just 2 examples amongst open models, no idea what closed models do but I am quite sure it's a lot closer to "RAG" than most sensationalist twitter ragebaiters account for !

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
After a few months of doing much AI coding for LLM research at Meta, here are my 2 cents.
tl;dr: Efficiency has now become much more about great parallelization than fast sequential execution. I find it super fun but for how long?
Setup: By default these past weeks, I was trying at every given time of the day/night/weekend to have as many signal-bearing training runs running on GPUs (the limit being my brain and slurm queues) + multiple Claude Code sessions working in the background on ~mildly useful things / side ideas / moonshots / unit tests. When I worked "actively", I usually just added a main Claude Code + IDE for high prio or critical work that needed more supervision or me coding. I was always waiting on something, so there was this constant guilt when going to lunch/sleep/coffee and no Claude Code was running async to me chilling. My schedule was conditionned on waiting for one more run to finish or for a code edit to be written, to then be able to launch the next one before departing from my laptop.
In the short term, the speedup is very clear. The biggest difference for me was not so much speed on my main task, but breadth: it became possible to test out/build/improve tons of things which I would never had prioritized before because I always had more urgent stuff to test out - or that the necessary boilerplate was boring me in advance. Now this runs async for free. Beyond experimental ideas, it is now virtually free to create beautiful figures, or even code your own custom experiment tracker which was never worth it before so the overall quality of the work improves on some axes as a free lunch.
I felt my role was more about being an continuous idea generator conditioned by a deep understanding of the experiments: the goal was to be able to as quickly as possible launch follow-ups and iteratively build understanding once results come in and repeat. I feel intuition is even more key as we don't really have N days of coding to reflect upon past iterations, and bottlenecks have shifted away from execution. Personally I love it, the barrier to "hard" things is lowered and creativity is left which is what I feel is the best part of my job.
Not sure how long this "phase" will last - contrary to many colleagues, I believe good research ideas + reflecting and reacting to experiments will soon be well within reach of LLMs . It has already stopped being fun for those who just love to code. For me it's the most fun I ever had building things and testing stuff, but for how long before my edge will be elsewhere (if anywhere) ?
I am now going back to writing my thesis, wrapping up paper writing and preparing interviews... Not having agents in the background kinda feels weird but I also appreciate the slower pace. Let's see how this all evolves!

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
summary:
Prod requires good infra, and mostly everything around vector search structured around FAISS historically. Making multivector practical often requires heavy compression, 2-stage retrieve + rerank approaches which is more engineering for sure. Support is still far from at the level single-vec has, but it has been slowly improving recently. I know first hand that there is quite a huge tax to changing existing infra, my old company was heavy on elastic and it is super expensive to change to something else (before elastic supported LI). Even now, support is often partial or not prod ready.
One more thing is I think people like having control over their "single vector collection": get them through APIs, manage them yourself in your DB. For true optimizations, it's better when the LI operation is hosted by the embedding provider (less bandwidth, GPU optims, pruning, efficient reranking). All to say there definitely is more friction but it's getting better for everyday users (in part due to great libs maintained by @raphaelsrty).
Last point is that it is often also possible to close the gap with single-vec models if you train them on domain specific data - and if you make sure queries are quite granular through an agentic scaffold / documents are not too long. A lot of the benchmarks where LI outshines single vec by a lot contain many quite extractive or multipart questions, which are not always representative of real world use (but may be).

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
clean_title: ViDoRe V3 accepted to ACL 2026 with strong practitioner support
summary:
ViDoRe V3 has been accepted to ACL 2026! Much more relevant however are the many practitioners I met in recent days that praised the benchmark for it's quality and clean signal. It's not easy making a good retrieval benchmark (non-saturated, practical, wide domain coverage) but it helps having done 2 imperfect earlier iterations, understanding what is needed, and having 12k hours of human annotation (thanks @NVIDIAAI ) + 6 months of hard work from notably @MaceQuent1
@antonio_loison @antoine_edy) amongst others.
From a scientific perspective, I believe we converged to a nice recipe that scales but remains challenging by mixing careful taxonomy design (@omrani_bilel), synthetic pre-annotations, and humans in many parts of the loop. This is by no means a cheap project - and going forward, non-trivial benchmarks will probably be more and more expensive. Gone are the days where using a LLM to annotate data creates a sufficient proxy for model improvement (ViDoRe V1).
Some people asked me when ViDoRe V4 would be out. I would assume this should not come from us - we are reaching the limits of data annotation, what we need now are fully real queries and real documents from real users of VDR (and more generally IR) models. This comes with data privacy issues and is tough but I believe it should be the north star - too many datasets in IR are completely toy and optimizing them actually hurts the model.
In all cases, ViDoRe V3 has a lot more to offer than just VDR (agents, RAG, etc) and should have at least a few months of non-saturation ahead of it!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFZWVTXWIAA116y.jpg
clean_summary:
ViDoRe V3 has been accepted to ACL 2026. Many practitioners praised the benchmark for its quality and clean signal, highlighting the challenges of creating a good retrieval benchmark that is non-saturated and has wide domain coverage. This success comes after two earlier iterations and 12,000 hours of human annotation, thanks to @NVIDIAAI, along with six months of hard work from contributors like @MaceQuent1, @antonio_loison, and @antoine_edy.

The project combines careful taxonomy design, synthetic pre-annotations, and human input, making it a costly endeavor. Moving forward, creating non-trivial benchmarks will likely become more expensive, as relying solely on LLMs for data annotation is no longer sufficient. While some have inquired about ViDoRe V4, the focus should now be on gathering real queries and documents from actual users, despite the associated data privacy challenges. ViDoRe V3 offers more than just VDR and is expected to maintain a non-saturated state for several months.

summary:
The arch here is a pretrained MoE decoder repurposed as a bidirectional encoder for token classification tasks (PII filtering).
For such tasks (as opposed to reasoning), parametric knowledge encoded in the FFN layers is super important, and the MoE arch enables to scale this without hindering efficiency. I had never really thought of the fact most encoder tasks are quite knowledge heavy and thus well correlated to what MoE unlocks.
(MoE encoder are not new ofc, many people have trained some)
clean_summary: The architecture discussed is a pretrained mixture of experts (MoE) decoder repurposed as a bidirectional encoder for token classification tasks, such as personally identifiable information (PII) filtering. For these tasks, parametric knowledge encoded in the feedforward network layers is crucial, and the MoE architecture allows for scaling this knowledge without sacrificing efficiency. This highlights the correlation between knowledge-heavy encoder tasks and the capabilities that MoE provides.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse)
clean_title: Importance of scaffolding in search results and LLM performance
summary:
I feel what these results (@mattjustram) mainly show is NOT that retrievers like BM25 are better than previously thought, NOT that GPT 5.5 is amazing at search orchestration, but rather that scaffolds matter a lot in search (and should be reported).
Pi-serini is one of the first non-trivial search specific efforts to give some proper tooling to LLMs (cached results, well defined tool calls) and smashes the baseline with the same retriever and baseline model. @antoine_chaffin 's results with/without the "get_document" tool also vastly differ: purely scaffolding. CC and Codex are good scaffolds by design and also perform very well at search as shown here (although they are not built specifically for this).
What does this mean:
Biggest low hanging fruits right now in search probably aren't through better embedding models (or even better baseline LLMs) but smart scaffolding paradigms (think RLMs @a1zhang, Pi-serini @lintool, Deep Research systems @din0s_ ).
As LLMs get better, I would expect inductive biases cooked in the scaffolds to become less important than now. However, scaffolds will still need to be expressive enough to let the baseline model "cook" and still need to encode what matters to the end user (speed matters a lot, search is not just accuracy).
Importantly, I believe scaffolds are not an inference time thing only, but should serve during document indexing. To properly contextualize documents in a corpus, we need to move away from the "1 paragraph/webpage is 1 document" concept and use agents to properly map the corpus space, and leverage their priors to index then retrieve. Test time compute scaling is not reserved to querying agents!
Just a few thoughts on recent results, this direction will be well aided by novel datasets like @dianetc_ 's Obliq-Bench which will necessarily require a change in paradigms, the easiest surely being around scaffolding.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HILypbsW8AAujM9.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HILypaZW8AAeSOa.jpg
clean_summary:
I feel what these results mainly show is that scaffolds matter a lot in search and should be reported. Pi-serini is one of the first non-trivial search-specific efforts to provide proper tooling to LLMs (cached results, well-defined tool calls) and significantly surpasses the baseline with the same retriever and model. @antoine_chaffin's results with and without the 'get_document' tool also differ vastly, highlighting the importance of scaffolding.

The biggest low-hanging fruits in search likely aren't through better embedding models or baseline LLMs but rather through smart scaffolding paradigms. As LLMs improve, the inductive biases in scaffolds may become less critical, but they will still need to be expressive enough for the baseline model to function effectively and to meet user needs, such as speed and accuracy. Scaffolds should also play a role during document indexing, moving away from the concept of '1 paragraph/webpage is 1 document' to using agents for better corpus mapping. This direction will be supported by novel datasets like @dianetc_'s Obliq-Bench, which will necessitate a change in paradigms, particularly around scaffolding.

title: Manuel Faysse (@ManuelFaysse) — thread (7 tweets)
clean_title: Self-Pruned KV attention for improved LLM memory efficiency
summary:
[1/7] 🚨 Do LLMs need to store everything they read in memory?
To reduce KV cache size and improve decoding speeds, we propose Self-Pruned KV attention, a mechanism where the model learns to decide which KVs to write in the persistent KV cache, discarding all the rest! @AIatMeta🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWW3oYXsAEUeZm.jpg
────────
[2/7] SP-KV works by predicting for each attention key how useful it will be in the future. Only keys above a threshold are kept and considered in the attention operation down the line! Importantly, KVs from the last 128 tokens are always kept to preserve local interactions! (2/N)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWW4CmWIAEmf4w.jpg
────────
[3/7] The cool part is that the utility prediction module is learned implicitly & jointly during LLM pretraining (or CPT): we don't incentivize sparsity, we just give the model the option to forget stuff. If it helps, it implicitly learns to do so and inversely (3/N)
────────
[4/7] Does this impact performance? Scaling laws look exactly the same as vanilla GQA attention, and so do downstream pretraining benchmarks, using only a fraction (15-35%) of the memory! Here, SP-KV is applied to pretrained models during a phase of CPT. (4/N)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWW4n1WgAEObPI.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWW4ssXQAAfxtA.jpg
────────
[5/7] One exception is a slight drop in RULER 32k performance. Our training mix has little long context data and we posit the SP-KV mechanism is not used to this regime. Adding long context data to the training mix enables to recover performance and shows SP-KV adapts well! (5/N)
────────
[6/7] We show memory "density" and performance is a tradeoff we can control at train/test time, and that beyond memory savings, sparser KV caches directly translate to increased throughputs during iterative decoding! (6/N)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWW5SXWwAE_8Ds.jpg
────────
[7/7] This paper is really a thorough exploration of this mechanism, and contains tons (really) of ablations, comparisons, and side explorations that I might tweet about later, but nothing beats checking it out directly! (7/N)
clean_summary:
Do LLMs need to store everything they read in memory? To reduce KV cache size and improve decoding speeds, Self-Pruned KV attention is proposed, where the model learns to decide which KVs to write in the persistent KV cache, discarding the rest.

SP-KV predicts the future utility of each attention key, keeping only those above a threshold while always retaining KVs from the last 128 tokens to preserve local interactions. This utility prediction module is learned implicitly during LLM pretraining, allowing the model to forget information when beneficial.

Performance scaling laws remain consistent with vanilla GQA attention, using only 15-35% of the memory, although there is a slight drop in RULER 32k performance due to limited long context data in training. The SP-KV mechanism adapts well when long context data is added, showing that sparser KV caches can increase throughput during iterative decoding.

title: Mustafa Shukor (@MustafaShukor1)
summary:
We’re pushing robotics’ boundaries at @UMA_Robots , grounded in decades of scientific research, scalable learning, and real-world experience !
Quoting @psermanet
I’m really happy to share that we’re launching UMA.
Together with @RemiCadene, @alibert_s, @therobotstudio, and an exceptional founding team, we’re building general-purpose mobile and humanoid robots. If you want to be part of this adventure, reach out at
Throughout my career, I have been obsessed with scalable learning and data acquisition methods that require little to no labels.
Back in 2005 with @ylecun, we were self-supervising our “deep” 2-layer network to do long range vision using short range stereo information, this was running live onboard our robot. However, because our deep model was so slow, the robot would crash constantly, so I designed a decoupled fast & far architecture for robust navigation, allowing fast control to coexist with slow long horizon thinking, much like systems 1 & 2 in modern humanoids.
My PhD was focused on making deep learning work for computer vision, including unsupervised feature learning with @koraykv, writing and open-sourcing a C++ deep learning library with @soumithchintala, and open-sourcing one of the first deep learning vision systems.
I came back towards robotics at @Google Brain and @GoogleDeepMind, where I pushed for entirely label-free methods on real robots. In 2017, @coreylynch and I managed to make our robot imitate human motion by co-training self-supervision across sim and real domains jointly, without any labels. With @imkelvinxu and @svlevine , we showed that unsupervised visual reward learning could be used for RL in the real world.
In 2020, Corey and I developed the first manipulation VLA, which was trained with very few language labels thanks to self-supervision on play data (playing is an efficient way to demonstrate and practice a broad set of skills and is essential for human development).
I was never satisfied with the status quo of top-down data collection, where researchers decide a few tasks to collect data on. Instead, I believed that we should let the data speak: tasks should be automatically discovered bottom-up (scalable and general) from cheap and continuous data collection, with a sprinkle of more expensive data and labels.
In 2022, I explored long-horizon reasoning for robotics using scalable automatic labeling augmentations for VQA tasks and studied the economics of different data collection schemes.
Most recently, I developed approaches to scalably discover laws of robotics from real data (images, hospital reports, sci-fi literature) in a broad and bottom-up fashion, which improved robot behavior over top-down approaches like Asimov’s laws.
All these experiences nourished my vision for UMA as Chief Scientist, I’m incredibly excited to put everything together and so grateful I get to contribute to this incredible moment in human history.
Picture: Yann supporting UMA as an advisor and investor, with the team in Paris a couple weeks ago.

title: Rohan Jha (@Robro612) — thread (12 tweets)
clean_title: Replicating XTR: A multi-vector retrieval method for faster ColBERT
summary:
[1/12] New 📄: we replicate XTR, a multi-vector retrieval method that makes ColBERT faster by avoiding its expensive step of gathering full document embeddings
XTR is not a free lunch over ColBERT, but its training objective is useful for modern efficient engines like PLAID and WARP 👇🏼
────────
[2/12] Refresher: XTR speeds up retrieval by skipping the costly step of gathering full document embeddings, instead it imputes missing MaxSim scores from initial token retrieval.
To make this work, XTR trains under a modified objective that simulates the sparser retrieval setting.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2cLrXIAUcMLC.jpg
────────
[3/12] One challenge: only one XTR checkpoint was released, without training code. So later works often benchmark XTR-style modifications (e.g. WARP) using either that single model, an unpaired ColBERT model. No controlled open ColBERT/XTR comparison.
────────
[4/12] We first replicate both parts of the recipe: XTR's token retrieval procedure and its modified contrastive objective.
────────
[5/12] We don’t replicate the claim that XTR strictly outperforms ColBERT in fact, quite the opposite. However XTR training does achieve better performance than ColBERT-as-XTR in the highly efficient (low k') regime.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2cuPXAAkyvml.jpg
────────
[6/12] Next, we extend XTR to a more modern setting: distillation & IVF retrieval engines like PLAID and WARP.
Here, XTR training matters more. It improves retrieval quality and makes WARP feasible. Distillation training ColBERT leads to unusable performance on WARP.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2dIXXsAI8kf2.jpg
────────
[7/12] We also find another benefit: XTR achieves lower latency *even on the same engine* when compared to ColBERT
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2daOXEAMYPjd.jpg
────────
[8/12] This is due to the compactness of XTR's candidate sets.
For example, in one FiQA setting, XTR reaches strong quality with ~10k candidates where the comparable ColBERT setup needs ~15k, echoing recent work by @fmnardini et al.:
────────
[9/12] Why? Evidence suggests XTR makes better use of the token embedding space, though lower anisotropy alone does not fully explain the effect.
This yields matches of higher quality —less purely lexical, more semantic— and a more discriminative score range.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2dxlWkAcPwdA.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2dxpXMAc_iKF.jpg
────────
[10/12] Takeaway: XTR's objective is broadly useful for efficient late-interaction retrieval, with efficiency benefits that will generalize across IVF-based indexes like PLAID, WARP, and newer systems like the Pisa group's TACHIOM.
────────
[11/12] Fortunately, thanks to the diligent work of open-source GOATs @antoine_chaffin @raphaelsrty @hugemensa, XTR and WARP are now integrated into PyLate.
Trying it yourself should be as simple as swapping the score function during training and the index at inference.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj2eN_WAAMs-1T.jpg
────────
[12/12] Paper:
Code:
Models:
Collaboration with @magmar_11 and @ben_vandurme
clean_summary:
New research replicates XTR, a multi-vector retrieval method that enhances ColBERT's efficiency by avoiding the costly step of gathering full document embeddings. XTR achieves this by imputing missing MaxSim scores from initial token retrieval, using a modified training objective that simulates a sparser retrieval setting.

The study finds that while XTR does not strictly outperform ColBERT, it performs better than ColBERT-as-XTR in low-efficiency scenarios. Additionally, XTR shows improvements in retrieval quality and lower latency compared to ColBERT, making it beneficial for modern retrieval engines like PLAID and WARP. The takeaway is that XTR's objective is broadly useful for efficient late-interaction retrieval across various systems.

The work also integrates XTR and WARP into PyLate, simplifying their implementation for users.

title: Yichuan Wang (@YichuanM) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] (1/N) 🚀 DS-Serve is a framework for efficient, scalable neural retrieval — it turns any in-house dataset (<1T tokens) into a high-throughput (up to 10,000 QPS), low-latency (<100ms), memory-efficient (<200GB RAM) retrieval system with a web UI and API.
With DS-Serve, we publicly deployed a 400B-token datastore of high-quality LLM pretraining data (2B vectors), spanning academic resources — and it matches commercial search endpoints on our benchmarks at extremely low latency and high throughput.
Try it out:
Blog:
Work from UC Berkeley ( @BerkeleyNLP & @BerkeleySky) with collaborators at UW & UIUC!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/G7_MYZVagAMdBkL.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/G7_MYZVagAMdBkL.mp4
────────
[2/4] (2/N) Why was scaling neural retrieval previously challenging? ⚡️
Neural retrieval at scale is unforgiving: you need throughput + accuracy + low memory—simultaneously. Linear scan dies instantly, and many open-source setups hit a wall past small-to-mid scale.
ANN comes with sharp tradeoffs: IVFPQ can lose quality (quantization) or pay in latency, while HNSW-style graphs can be RAM-hungry and painful to build.
────────
[3/4] (3/N) DS-Serve Under the Hood: The Tech 🔧
A key component of DS Serve is DiskANN. Its graph based, memory efficient indexing is the solution to the scale challenges from the last post, delivering strong accuracy with low latency, high throughput, and modest RAM in our tests (vs IVFPQ, etc.).
We then put it to work in a public demo on CompactDS (380B words, ~2B vectors) spanning web crawl, Wikipedia, research papers, and more:
────────
[4/4] (6/N) 🚀 Index showdown: DiskANN vs. IVFPQ. We directly compare accuracy + latency, and DiskANN is a clear win. At recommended configs, DiskANN delivers ~2.3× higher throughput and ~2.2× lower latency—while also being more accurate.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7_Mdlra8AA5Atl.png

clean_summary:
🚀 DCI just hit #1 on Hugging Face Daily Papers. It replaces the entire agentic search pipeline—embedding model, vector index, top-k retrieval—with simple tools like grep and bash.

The approach allows the agent to search the raw corpus directly using shell commands, without preprocessing, embedding models, or offline indexing. It outperforms top baselines across 13 benchmarks, with average gains of +11.0% in agentic search, +30.7% in multi-hop QA, and +21.5% in IR ranking.

Controlled ablation studies identify the sources of DCI’s improvements, focusing on trajectory-level search, evidence utilization, context management, and tool usage. The method demonstrates that effective retrieval can be achieved with minimal tools, unlocking new possibilities for agentic search systems.

title: alex zhang (@a1zhang)
summary:
on the naming choice of RLMs
it’s fair to say that RLMs aren’t a new architecture / new NN, so the naming is confusing. it was a point of discussion with my advisor @lateinteraction when we were exploring this idea a few months back. I think though that what we think of as a “model” can be reframed beyond just a NN
ultimately a big goal and motivation for the naming is to challenge the idea that a Transformer / NN is the lowest level abstraction of a “language model”. LMs are great & have gotten us very far, but we’re getting to the regime where they’re very expensive to improve. increasing physical context windows is a million dollar endeavor. hillclimbing benchmarks like SWE-bench is becoming a billion dollar endeavor. but it’s sort of limiting to always talk abt the performance of these base models when they can improve significantly in a task-agnostic way with a bit of extra scaffolding
I am very excited by the idea of RLMs being used as drop-in replacements for LM calls. It’s why a big focus of our experiments is on RLM vs. LM performance for 1) tasks that fit in the context window of an LM and 2) tasks that do not. In this way, I think of an RLM as a base model of sorts (mathematically this is a totally reasonable view btw), but I understand the general hesitation to view it this way.
atp tho I still agree and figured the naming might turn some heads, but what’s done is done 😮‍💨

title: alex zhang (@a1zhang)
summary:
Maybe I can provide some intuition, but lmk if it’s unclear — I am trying to refine how I explain this anyways!
To start, I think the RLM idea is super simple but elegant (I'm biased obviously). The paper argues that future “language models” 1) do not need to think about context window limits; 2) will have “reasoning” chains that mix code (symbolic) and neural LMs (fuzzy). RLMs are what we think minimally such a system should look like. Explicitly, it is an LM <—> REPL + prompt, where the REPL contains the prompt and sub-agents as a *function inside the REPL*. This last part is quite important, because it implies that 1) an RLM can launch sub-agents as if they were functions inside of an algorithm or program, and 2) we can prevent any single neural LM call from having to deal with context rot or huge contexts.
The line between a coding agent and an RLM is hazy because coding agent just means LM + code (The REPL used in an RLM doesn’t even need to be a coding environment, but this is a detail not relevant to this argument). But most standard coding agent implementations do not do what I described above, and explicitly use the “LM calls sub-agents as a tool” paradigm, which makes the REPL and sub-agent completely independent tools. It’s not the “sub-agent having access to a grepper” (as you’ve described) that matters at all, it’s that the sub-agent is called from and communicates inside of the REPL.
The point Omar makes about individual neural LM calls not needing to see everything is an important property of the system above, and it’s also why it naturally extends to enormous context problems (maybe using a grep + sub-call strategy, or something even more interesting). So in some sense yes, an RLM is our argument for the right way to write a “coding agent”, but I almost think this framing is unhelpful because it narrows the scope back to coding tasks. RLMs are task-agnostic (like ReAct, CodeAct, etc.), and code can be used for task-agnostic things. And I’m fairly confident that most future coding scaffolds will start to converge to these properties as well, but I think we should start thinking beyond that and apply these principles to non-coding tasks. BTW, I think @random_walker has a well-written tweet that argues something similar w.r.t. neurosymbolic AI, and it boils down to a lot of similar ideas.
Obviously I’m biased, but I like how the paper is written and think there’s a lot of good intuition (esp for those interested in *training*) to think about for what we want LM systems to look like in the future. The last thing I’ll mention is that the name “recursive LM” comes from the idea that an RLM can be trained by only training a singular LM with a fixed context window in this system, and in this way it is “recursively” calling itself.
Note on terminology:
Language model = any (probabilistic) mapping from text --> text. Ultimately this is what we really care about.
Neural language model = our standard Transformer / parameterized NN. LM doesn't *have* to be this.

title: alex zhang (@a1zhang)
clean_title: RLM builds interface to play Pokemon Red in under 5 hours
summary:
A fun 48-hour run of letting an RLM iteratively building the interface for an RLM to play Pokemon Red (sneak peak of some fun things cooking at @PrimeIntellect😄). The interface generating RLM was just tasked with getting the RLM (same scaffold) to beat the game in under 5 hours wall-clock time.
I originally expected the RLM to design some components used in Gemini Plays Pokemon like an extra map, an interface to parse the screen, etc., design low-level policies that would run fast on the emulator, and also design a good prompt and strategy around the RLM to use sub-agents to explore game state with checkpointing, use RNG manipulation in its favor, etc.
Instead the RLM eventually just decided to give the RLM a `write_memory` tool, which the RLM player decided to use to 1) warp the player immediately to the Elite 4; 2) give itself a level 100 Mewtwo (which it mistakes to be a Ponyta due to weird Pokedex ID vs. internal ID); 3) give itself $999999; 4) give itself all 8 badges by setting the right flag. It then went ahead and destroyed the Elite 4 and Blue and beat the game in record time :p
You'll also notice in the video there's weird backtracking and frame-skipping, this happens because it also did incorporate the strategy of launching sub-agents to explore action trajectories, but had a strange way of saving the frames and recording them (so you see the result of several sub-agent explorations).
We'll have some more funny and cool RLM demos soon, but it's cool to see RLMs work as general-purpose agents (both the coding agent that designs the interface and the game-playing agent itself)!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2055115708036530176/img/929hUdCYMHnvACMa.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2055115708036530176/vid/avc1/320x456/89y5r7EluQQ0Y2i2.mp4?tag=27
clean_summary:
A fun 48-hour run of letting a Reinforcement Learning Model (RLM) iteratively build the interface for another RLM to play Pokemon Red. The interface-generating RLM was tasked with getting the game-playing RLM to beat the game in under 5 hours of wall-clock time.

Instead of designing components like an extra map or low-level policies, the RLM decided to give the player a `write_memory` tool, which it used to warp to the Elite 4, give itself a level 100 Mewtwo, acquire $999999, and obtain all 8 badges. It then defeated the Elite 4 and Blue, beating the game in record time. The video shows some backtracking and frame-skipping due to the RLM's strategy of launching sub-agents to explore action trajectories. It's exciting to see RLMs work as general-purpose agents.

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
It is a very interesting study from @bclavie
As bullish as I am on multimodal RAG, it is important to acknowledge that we are not there yet
The retrieval part is honestly very good (maybe we are not testing on precise-enough text-heavy tasks though), but the reading part (and thus generation) is still far from perfect
On single page it is pretty okay, but real use cases will require more than one page and to combine them properly as well
We can and should obviously focus on making VLMs better on multi-page inputs, but a clear bottleneck is just reading text. It correlates pretty much with the claims of OCR being solved: it works on some cases, but it is far from perfect. Not decoding the latent space prevents some errors, but it does not do wonder either, we need to get better
Also, please note that this is a bench where text is "simply" casted into images. The resulting documents aren't that realistic/plausible. That was not the purpose of this study and you got to start somewhere, but this is the higher bound of the results. It should get worse with distractors (although maybe VLMs overfitted on LaTeX/Word and might actually be better, but I do not think so)

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
I'll be covering Reason-ModernColBERT in tonight's presentation, so please come if you are interested!
(And please be gentle, this is the first time I will be speaking live in front of this many people 😭)
Quoting @victorialslocum
Looking for a cheaper, open source alternative to agentic RAG?
Try multi-vector retrieval with Reason-ModernColBERT.
Most search systems compare one big summary vector per document. Multi-vector retrieval is different - it keeps separate vectors for each word or phrase, then finds the best matches between your search and the document pieces.
Reason-ModernColBERT is a small but mighty model trained on the reasonir-hq dataset and specializes in finding documents that require logical thinking, not just keyword matching.
It actually outperforms models 45x larger on reasoning tasks with just 150M parameters - tiny compared to billion-parameter models. It also creates small 128-dimension vectors and handles documents up to 8,000+ words long.
So while agentic RAG uses LLMs to tackle complex questions requiring intricate planning, multi-step reasoning, and utilization of external tools, sometimes you don't need all that complexity. Multi-vector retrieval gives you smart search results at a fraction of the cost.
Ready to try it? Check out this notebook by @helloiamleonie:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GvUuozNXcAAFbEl.png

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Should we just focus our pre-training efforts on decoders?
To answer this, we trained Ettin, various identically trained encoders and decoders, ranging from 17M to 1B parameters on 2T tokens of open data (beating Llama 3.2 and ModernBERT in the process)!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv_KGlYW0AAkPWi.jpg
Quoting @orionweller
🤔 Have you ever wondered how good ModernBERT is compared to decoders like Llama?
We made an open-data version of ModernBERT and used the same recipe for encoders and decoders.
Turns out, our encoder model beat ModernBERT and our decoder model beats Llama 3.2 / SmolLM2 🤯
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv_Io_xXsAAVOEd.jpg
────────
[2/3] You might have seen a similar paper recently by @gisship @N1colAIs and @ManuelFaysse
How do these studies compare?
Well, essentially, we scaled the training way further (100B vs 2T), and although some results differ, they can actually be connected
Essentially, they show that CLM is more data efficient (which makes sense, we only use x% of the data with MLM).Thus, in the "low" data regime, it makes sense that CLM+MLM is better than only MLM
However, when scaled, the inefficiency of MLM is flattened out and the actual edge of MLM starts to show
In their study, they also studied the ideal ratio of CLM/MLM to use. This is super interesting (although, as I said, I believe this might be different in a larger scale regime), but unfortunately, the realistic case is that we have available models that have been pre-trained on trillions of tokens, and reaching those ratios means further training on a very large amount of data
Thus, I believe our setup is more realistic, but their study raises very interesting questions as well
It is very nice to see people also questioning the status quo!
Finally, it is fair to point out two things in our results:
1. The trend for retrieval does not hold for the 1B model. While it could be argued that this indicates that the results do not hold for larger-scale models, our guess is rather that the 1B is only trained on a fraction of the data (due to cost) and thus the ratio between CLM and MLM is very different
2. The classification results for dec-to-enc are only reported for MNLI. While we think this task is representative of downstream classification results, it might hide some nuances
We'll surely run more experiments for the camera-ready, but as we are releasing _all_ the checkpoints, data, and using WSD, we encourage everyone to run the experiments they think are relevant!
────────
[3/3] I would like to really thanks @orionweller for leading this project, this kind of comparison is something I have dreamed about during my whole PhD
Also thanks to HF folks who helped for the release!
And obviously thanks to the whole ModernBERT team, which enabled this work!

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
Despite meming, I strongly believe information theory lens could solve a lot of things, including search
Quoting @max_spero_
I just read this new paper from Claude Shannon and I’m absolutely buzzing 🤯
The core idea is almost offensively simple: define information as uncertainty, measure it in bits, and treat communication as the process of reducing that uncertainty. That’s it. And somehow…it unlocks a whole new regime of math, coding, and technology.
Here’s what blew my mind:
Information = surprise. Rare events carry more bits than common ones. Suddenly, probability isn’t just math—it’s the backbone of communication.
A channel has a capacity. Every medium—phone line, fiber optic, wireless—has a hard throughput ceiling you can calculate.
Noise is real, but beatable. With clever encoding, you can push arbitrarily close to the limit while still decoding correctly. Error correction isn’t a hack, it’s inevitable and essential.
Compression formalized. Redundancy can be removed with mathematics, not just tricks. JPEGs, ZIP files, streaming codecs—this is the blueprint.
Universality. Language, music, DNA, stock data—if it’s symbols with probabilities, Shannon’s framework applies.
Why this matters (right now):
Limits → strategy. Knowing the ceiling means you design to it. Wireless, storage, streaming—all of them are being rebuilt on this math.
Coding → product. From 5G to data centers to error-correcting RAM, Shannon’s theory translates directly into real-world wins.
Abstraction → leverage. Stop thinking medium-by-medium. Think in entropy and bits. One framework, all domains.
What I’m changing this week:
Running every “data” question through an entropy lens: how much surprise is really there?
Revisiting compression and coding research with Shannon’s math fresh in my head. It feels like everything is still downstream of this.
Asking “what’s the capacity?” before touching implementation—because if you don’t know the limit, you can’t know if you’re close.
This paper feels like an inflection point. If you’re building anything with communication, storage, or computation—read it, internalize it, and rethink your roadmap. The title isn’t just academic. A Mathematical Theory of Communication really is the operating manual for the digital age.

(1/n) 🚨 BERTs that chat: turn any BERT into a chatbot with diffusion
hi @karpathy, we just trained a few BERTs to chat with diffusion — we are releasing all the model checkpoints, training curves, and recipes! Hopefully this spares you the side quest into training nanochat with diffusion for now 🙂. It’s both a hands-on tutorial for beginners and an example showing how to use our complete toolkit (dLLM) for deeper projects.
Code:
Report:
Checkpoints:
Motivation: I couldn’t find a good “Hello World” example for training a minimally working yet useful diffusion language models, a class of bidirectional language models capable of parallel token generation in arbitrary order. TLDR: With a small amount of open-source instruction-following data, a standard BERT can gain conversational ability with diffusion. Specifically, a finetuned ModernBERT-large, with a similar number of parameters, performs close to Qwen1.5-0.5B.

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin) — thread (14 tweets)
summary:
[1/14] Your coding agent is burning tokens on grep like it's 1973
Because semantic search means remote APIs & babysitting an index
Introducing ColGrep & LateOn-Code
SOTA code retrieval with lightweight models.
Wins 70% vs grep. 15.7% less tokens.
Local, open & free. Runs on a toaster.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA-AkOKX0AAAdvl.jpg
────────
[2/14] Blog post:
HF collection:
Start saving token today:
We release everything, the models, the training data, the recipes and most importantly, ColGrep, the harness to enhance your agent and save tokens
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA-AoMEbsAIdrXG.jpg
────────
[3/14] Agents waste thousands of tokens doing trial-and-error grep. They guess identifiers, refine patterns, grep again, read wrong files and backtrack
When a query is "where is the caching logic?" and the function is called `_build_lru_store`, grep has no chance on the first try
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA-BB4RbAAAjTLS.jpg
────────
[4/14] ColBERT-style models keep per-token representations instead of crushing everything into one vector
Soft-matching power of embeddings + fine-grained matching of lexical search
Perfect for code, where there's rigid structure but intent and syntax rarely share the same words
────────
[5/14] We pre-trained models on the CoRNStack data and then further refined them using nv-retriever negatives on the CoIR train sets
The smaller model, based on the 17M ColBERT model from @mixedbreadai outperforms 149M models (9x bigger), only falling short of EmbeddingGemma-300M
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA-BJ6IWIAAm-Js.jpg
────────
[6/14] The bigger one is based on our (soon-to-be-released) in-house LateOn model is strongly outperforms EmbeddingGemma-300M and is competing with LLMs of 500-600M while being only 149M
Both models punch way above their weight and are small enough to run locally
────────
[7/14] "Nice benchmarks. Does it work in practice?"
Agents know grep, so ColGrep keeps the interface and add semantic ranking on top
Regex finds idiomatic retry patterns while semantic ranking surfaces intent about backoff logic
grep's precision + embedding's understanding
────────
[8/14] Agents go wild with this and have no issue leveraging its effectiveness
We ran 135 questions (variable difficulty) across 7 repos
Answers generated with ColGrep were preferred 70% of the time, while using 15.7% fewer tokens on average and using 56% less search operations
────────
[9/14] Tokens aren’t free
On our 135 questions bench, we saved around 32$
As a rule of thumb, this means 243$/1k question
It starts to add up pretty quickly, especially given large team usages
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA-BftHXIAAuGLn.jpg
────────
[10/14] The most satisfying result is that the biggest gains are on the hardest questions that describe behavior, not function names, where embeddings really shines

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
It is actually a large debate in the community for some time
Essentially, @bcherny said back then (and is still emphasizing it) that they tried to use embeddings-based RAG back then for Claude Code and that essentially it was wasteful because agents were finding the things through trial and error with grep
Thus, it would not be worth bothering with the additional layer of complexity brought by embeddings, especially because it would mean privacy issues (sending the data over) and you also need to keep your index up-to-date, which can be painful. This is the PoV shared by @cline
However, @cursor_ai noted that embeddings were actually useful, especially with larger code bases. On our side, we definitely noticed that they were useful, greatly speeding up search when there was semantic/intent behind the original query, and, for very complex query, it finds things that it could not have found with just "blind" search
We believe ColGrep is kind of the best of both worlds:
thanks to the awesome performance of late interaction models, we can have very good results with a 17M model. Through quant and ONNX, it means that you can have something that runs locally (so no privacy issues) at lightspeed (so no issue for keeping index in sync)
Besides, late interaction models works at the token level, which works *very* well with the iterative behavior of agent, so we plug nicely
Add to that the actual extension of the original grep tool/capabilities, and you have something that solves a lot of problems and plug nicely in existing setups!

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin) — thread (19 tweets)
summary:
[1/19] State-of-the-art ColBERT models are trained by applying knowledge distillation on top of dense pre-trained models
What if we run the whole pre-training in the multi-vector?
Introducing ColBERT-Zero, a model that sets a new SOTA on BEIR, using only public data
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiGPZZWYAAXpWn.jpg
────────
[2/19] Blogpost:
Collection:
Paper:
Code:
This work is a collaboration between @LightOnIO and @EPFL_en!
────────
[3/19] There are 3 training phases for retrieval models:
1. Unsupervised contrastive pre-training (massive pair only data, very expensive)
2. Supervised contrastive fine-tuning (mined hard negatives, smaller data)
3. Knowledge distillation from a teacher model
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiGcezXAAEcAgE.jpg
────────
[4/19] Most ColBERT models only do phase 3 on top of models that performed the first two phases in a single vector setting
But is this really enough?
To explore this, we leverage the well known work of Nomic Embed and compare different setups
────────
[5/19] We compare three setups:
(a). Only applying KD on top of the dense model they trained (usual setup)
(b). Applying the supervised phase and the KD on top of their unsupervised dense model
(c). Running the full pre-training in the ColBERT setting (ColBERT-Zero)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiGiGiWgAEXZ4W.jpg
────────
[6/19] The results are very clear: ColBERT-zero, the fully pre-trained model hits 55.43 nDCG@10, strongly outperforming the previous ColBERT SOTA GTE-ModernColBERT (54.67) and even its dense base model gte-modernbert (55.33)
As a matter of fact, ColBERT-zero outperforms any <150M model
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiGlTfX0AAz76Y.jpg
────────
[7/19] These results confirm that a simple distillation step is insufficient for optimal multi-vector performance.
The dense baseline trained on Nomic data scores 52.89, while the one trained on GTE's proprietary data scores 55.33.
Despite this initial 2.4-point disadvantage in data quality, the full ColBERT pre-training pipeline allows ColBERT-Zero to overcome the gap
On the other hand, the KD-only approach scores 54.09, lagging behind full pre-training by 1.3 points
────────
[8/19] But running the full pre-training is expensive, with the vast majority spent on the unsupervised phase
Luckily, we find that running only the supervised phase before the KD yields very close results for a fraction of the cost: 10× cheaper for 99.4% of the performance
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiGwUVWcAAhs55.jpg
────────
[9/19] Another critical finding: prompt alignment is non-negotiable
If your base model was pre-trained with specific prompts, you MUST keep them during fine-tuning
Stripping them tanks performance and adding them when they weren't there during pre-training also hurts
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiG0deXoAAHMKX.jpg
────────
[10/19] However, the prompts seems useful besides simple pre-training alignment, as when running full pre-training in both setups, we see a large advantage for model leveraging prompt
So why is that? Well, we ran A BUNCH of ablations to try to disentangle different effects
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiG4AOW0AEoaUt.png
────────
[11/19] It seems that both the prompts themselves and the increased query/document lengths we use to account for them are useful, and both are additive, especially on ColBERT-pre-trained models
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBiG7YYXcAALEvs.jpg
────────
[12/19] Our hypothesis is that prompt tokens act as query expansion, a mechanism that was shown to be very useful in the early version but is not used in modern models leveraging Flash Attention because FA outputs zeros/NaN embeddings for masked tokens (yes, this issue, AGAIN)
────────
[13/19] Please note that we used Nomic setup to ground our findings in a well-established setup, it also means some observations may not generalize to different or stronger training configurations
The results are less about the objective of each phase, but rather their strength/scale
Indeed, knowledge distillation typically improves results after supervised fine-tuning. The fact that a prior contrastive phase further enhances performance suggests that these gains are less about the specific objective and more about the scale of training
The goal of this study, however, was to explore the conventional setup where training scale is inversely proportional to signal quality, reflecting the higher cost of generating high-quality labels
────────
[14/19] As usual, we're releasing everything under Apache 2.0: all models (including intermediate checkpoint and prompt exploration) and PyLate training scripts
📦 Models:
💻 Code:
📄 Paper:
────────
[15/19] Now that we showed that we can reach SOTA with non-SOTA data, what would happen if we ran these training with stronger data?
Guess we'll find out very soon 👀
────────
[16/19] Time for thanks and cc!
Big thanks to the amazing guys from the @EPFL_en for working with us on the project, @l_arnaboldi and @KrzakalaF (particular shoutout to Luca for bearing with all my ablations requests)
Also big thanks to my boss, @AmelieTabatta for helping making this project come as clean as it is now, especially when ablations were depressing (and also for making such cute graphs)

Also thanks to @tomaarsen, for reviewing the BP but also for maintaining ST. The work would not exist without PyLate, but PyLate would not exist without ST

It's really inspiring and we'll soon make your work last in another way!

claude code has a hidden setting that makes it 600x faster and almost nobody knows about it
by default it uses text grep to find functions.
it doesn't understand your code at all. that's why it takes 30-60 seconds and sometimes returns the wrong file
there's a flag called ENABLE_LSP_TOOL that connects it to language servers. same tech that powers vscode's ctrl+click to jump straight to the definition
after enabling it:

> "fix the auth bug on my dashboard" - traces the actual call hierarchy instead of guessing which file handles auth
> after every edit it auto-catches type errors immediately instead of you finding them 10 prompts later
also saves tokens because claude stops wasting context searching for the wrong files
2 minute setup and it works for 11 languages

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
CDE is really awesome and Jack is the goat (seeing IR through the information theory lens and what CDE actually implies is still undermined imho)
However, I feel like this particular article makes something actually hard looks like it's trivial
Yes, in theory, you just have to gather samples, mine hard negatives and filter false ones in the process
This is exactly what we did and yes, it improves the performance/yields state-of-the-art models, but it takes much more to really go further. It takes a lot of looking at the data and ablating what works and what doesn't, in a space where evaluations are more noisy than a techno festival
In some sense, this is very much related to generating synthetic data (some could argue that even without generating queries, generating pseudo labels is "synthetic data" in some sense). It indeed helps and allows to reach new high, but it's nowhere near easy or straightforward
And even if it's probably one of the most useful work to do (when you then openly release the data), it's not fun at all for the vast majority of people
Messing around with new methods (such as CDE) is imho much more fun and can really break what's possible, as opposed of just training on more data

title: BrowseComp-Plus, perhaps the hardest popular deep research task, is now solved at nearly 90%... ... and all it took was a 150M model ✨ Thrilled to announce that — thread (16 tweets)
summary:
[1/16] 📷 BrowseComp-Plus, perhaps the hardest popular deep research task, is now solved at nearly 90%... ... and all it took was a 150M model ✨ Thrilled to announce that Reason-ModernColBERT did it again and outperform all models (including models 54× bigger) on all metrics
────────
[2/16] Model:
If you are not familiar with the model, it is a multi-vector model built at @LightOnIO optimized for reasoning-intensive retrieval, outperforming model 45x bigger on the BRIGHT benchmark
And now, it does it again, for agentic search/deep research
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDyEehfWQAA423T.jpg
────────
[3/16] Coupled to GPT-5, it reaches 87.59 accuracy, a 7.59 points improvement over previous best
But that's not all, it also tops recall (83.52% vs. 80.29%) AND calibration error (7.46 vs. 7.92) all at the same time (previous bests on each metric belonged to different runs)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDyEltqWEAAlUSe.jpg
────────
[4/16] But maybe even more impressive is that it does it while using few search calls, highlighting the quality of the search
Few search calls coupled with a small model means that we are getting those results while being extremely efficient
────────
[5/16] You might have noticed that there are two results for the model, it's because one uses a "non-standard" scaffold
Nothing fancy, it's literally just exposing a `get_document(id)` function so the LLM can fetch the full document when it wants to, that's it
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDyEzclaYAA_R_W.png
────────
[6/16] It's "non-standard" because the official scaffold is just exposing a search endpoint that returns the top-5 documents alongside the first 512 tokens for each
Allowing the model to read a full document if it thinks it's helpful is pretty standard and requires good retrieval signal to not rot the context of the model
────────
[7/16] We can see that this very simple scaffold (compared to more complex custom ones) is extremely effective with Reason-ModernColBERT and boosts the performance while reducing a lot the search calls
This highlights the quality of the retrieval signal
────────
[8/16] That being said, it's important to note that the results obtained using the standard scaffold are still very impressive, because it largely outperforms all the other standard runs and matches the best custom ones (that use much larger models)
────────
[9/16] Also ran the bench using GPT-OSS-120B and here again, Reason-ModernColBERT > Qwen3-8B-Embed, no matter the setup
Also ran GTE-ModernColBERT (the base ColBERT model), and we can see that, although the reasoning fine-tuning helped, a generic 150M ColBERT model outperforms Qwen3-8B
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDyFISzWwAEoTWY.jpg
────────
[10/16] Thus, it seems that the reasoning fine-tuning also helps for agentic search, but most of the performance lift seems to arise from using multi-vector models (similarly to the results on the BRIGHT benchmark)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDyFcfpXQAA4prC.jpg
────────
[11/16] Combined with the impressive results of LateOn-Code models and the ColGrep harness for coding agents, we can clearly see a trend where late interaction models seem particularly suited for this new agentic era
If you factor in the long context and out-of-domain generalization capabilities, you know the future will be very bright (pun intended)
────────
[12/16] This is an old model, but PyLate models are so strong, they keep getting new SOTA months after release (this is a perk of being late interaction models)
As usual, everything is open, code, data, models
Everything is a few lines of PyLate code trained in like 4 hours
Models links:
Training code:
────────
[13/16] If you want to start using late interaction models and you are familiar with dense models and sentence transformers, PyLate should be your next step
It is a library that extends ST to late interaction models, so the code is essentially the same (you can re-use your existing data/code/setups)
────────

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
Very cool blog post simply explaining smart ideas with great visualizations, love it!
Also, it seems that Cursor will slowly converge towards ColGrep (which is logical): an hybrid of regex augmented by semantic search that is efficient enough to run locally
Quoting @cursor_ai
Cursor can now search millions of files and find results in milliseconds.
This dramatically speeds up how fast agents complete tasks.
We're sharing how we built Instant Grep, including the algorithms and tradeoffs behind the design.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HEHCYEkXUAEyMnw.png

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
ColGrep solves the challenges of coding agent:
- It runs efficiently locally, so there is no issue of privacy and it makes keeping the index up to date much easier
- It doesn't replace grep that the agent loves to use, it extends it with semantic capabilities
- It uses multi-vector models, that works **very** well with the agentic search (iterative search that is keyword-ish)
Cursor noted that the gains of semantic search are there, especially for large codebases
But they also acknowledge that grep is very powerful (and suited to agents!)
> There are other state-of-the art techniques to gather context for Agents. We've talked in the past about how much you can improve Agent performance by using semantic indexes for many tasks, but there are specific queries which the model can only resolve by searching with regular expression
-> ColGrep allows to get the best of both worlds!
And they also acknowledge that using local indexes is the way forward
> Indexes for speeding up regular expression search need to live somewhere. All the designs we've seen so far have been deployed on the server side, and the semantic indexes we've talked about are also managed and queried on the server. And yet, we're choosing to go in a different direction here: we're building and querying the indexes in the users' machines.
-> LateOn-Code small and efficient models allows to go one step further and also run the semantic search locally!

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
summary:
ColBERT models are very easy to train/fine-tune
This paper highlights that one of the issue of dense bi-encoder training against cross encoder is that the factorized expression of cross encoder allows to only modify the couple representation and not be too noisy, while bi-encoder modify the representation of the documents _for all queries_ given a single training query
This is why ColBERT shines: the max operator selects only a few token representations to update (the ones that matched the query, and are thus related!) and keep the rest untouched, making the updates chirurgical and way less noisy
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HELqKmLXAAAb5Jk.jpg
Quoting @CShorten30
Late Interaction is not only great for inference, but also for training!! 🏭
Fine-tuning single-vector embedding models hasn’t really taken off… Late Interaction could change this.
One of my favorite takeaways from the podcast, here is a clip explaining this further in ~1 minute. 💡
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2036432337903177728/img/zYnniFIk9vTJ6fJ1.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2036432337903177728/vid/avc1/480x270/CKIG-JUIagKhjlDX.mp4?tag=21

summary:
Reminder that ColGrep is both 2 and 3
It's a tool that extends grep with the powerful late interaction model capabilities
It is actually the best way to make your agent faster, smarter and save a lot of $$$
Quoting @softwaredoug
Next Cheat at Search cohort is coming up May 18.
Here's my talk "What is agentic search?" But this video is 3 months old. What's new / different in the last few months?
First I think the expectation your search agent might generate code. Recursive Language Models, for example, that keep the entire context on a variable in a python REPL.
Second - the emphasis on grep'ing file system, not just regular search. All the little tools people use to manage context (grep, QMD, the many semantic greps)
Third - late interaction making strides. It feels like the awareness of late interaction techniques on agentic search benchmarks like BrowseComp-Plus. Even *tiny* late interaction models win. (You should be following @LightOnIO, @lateinteraction , @antoine_chaffin , @mixedbreadai , @bclavie to name a few)
2026 will be about everyone finding the retrieval tools that make agentic search efficient. That backed by a reasoning engine create very robust search capabilities inside and outside chat experiences

clean_title: LightOn releases DenseOn and LateOn models for improved retrieval
summary:
[1/22] The new generation of open state-of-the-art single and multi-vector retrieval models is here
It's time, DenseOn with the LateOn 🎶
@LightOnIO releases models that leap past existing ones, and everything you need to do the same!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcA4wQXsAA3mNk.jpg
────────
[2/22] Collection:
Blog:
We don't just release models that outperform every model their size and models 4× bigger, holding strong under decontamination
We also release the large-scale curated datasets and findings so you can do the same
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcBISXXsAAqEYK.jpg
────────
[3/22] DenseOn is the first <150M to beat the 56 mark on BEIR and even beats Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
LateOn is the first ColBERT to beat the 57 (and thus 56) mark, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art, ColBERT-Zero, by almost two points
More importantly, they still outperform all of these models when we remove any BEIR data that overlaps with our training data
But how did we get there? Let me tell you the whole story
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcBSLFWwAAGFpR.jpg
────────
[4/22] Capabilities of information retrieval models are evolving rapidly and most leaderboards are increasingly topped by closed models, either locked behind APIs or simply trained on closed data and having only open weights
This is damaging for various reasons
────────
[5/22] It prevents exploration of possible data leakage and contamination (or even purposely overfitting)
Even more importantly, it prevents broader exploration of new ideas and gatekeeps the demonstration of superior performance to a few private companies owning this data (which also puts academia at a strong disadvantage)
────────
[6/22] Nomic-embed released both the models and the data used to train them, which enabled a lot of cool and controlled studies (such as our ColBERT-Zero one)
Unfortunately, it has become outdated and we can see that, for example, GTE-ModernBERT, despite sharing the same backbone, is underperforming ModernBERT-embed
────────
[7/22] The mGTE report describes its data sources but doesn't release the data itself: reproducible in theory, painful in practice
Unless you're willing to suffer the pain of collecting everything
Which we decided to do
────────
[8/22] Today we release all the data sources (and more) in one place, more than 1.4B query-document pairs
Plus a new high-quality web dataset built on FineWeb-Edu, replacing the outdated "common crawl" splits most mixtures still rely on (thanks @orionweller)
────────
[9/22] Then we carefully curated it all
We developed per-source structural filters, applied deduplication and computed cross-encoder relevance on every pair
Crucially, every curation step is non-destructive
We keep all the data and expose filters as metadata, applied at training time
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcBtDUWQAEbJvh.jpg
────────
[10/22] We directly release the best mixture we found (alongside the values used to create it) to make usage easier
But again, we encourage everyone to swap our filters, add your own, etc. Feel free to explore!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcB0Q9XgAAlmSn.jpg
────────
[11/22] After the large-scale pairs pre-training, the next essential step is a refinement on smaller scale but higher quality datasets
We thus built fine-tuning datasets by mining the 2048 closest elements to find hard negatives following nv-retrieve setup for 1.88M queries
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcB5BCXEAAs9oa.jpg
────────
[12/22] Here again, everything is non destructive: we release all the 2048 closest elements alongside their retriever scores, which allows to use any threshold for nv-retrieve but also to use them in other setups (even knowledge distillation!)
────────
[13/22] Building on these findings, we built a proprietary Apache 2.0 compatible dataset to train DenseOn and LateOn
────────
[14/22] DenseOn hits 56.20 on BEIR, making it the top base-size dense retriever, and the first sub-150M model past 56
It beats GTE-ModernBERT (55.19), the main inspiration from this work using the same backbone. It also notably beats Arctic-Embed-L-v2 (568M) and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (595M) despite being ~4× smaller. It even stays very close to the recent and larger pplx-embed-v1 (596M) and jina-v5-text-nano (239M)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcCFS6WgAAoDGG.jpg
────────
[15/22] LateOn hits 57.22, the first ColBERT (and first sub-150M model) to break 57 on BEIR.
It beats the previous SOTA, ColBERT-Zero (55.32) by nearly 2 points and GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 by 2.5, despite sharing the same backbone.
And this is without prompts and KD. It means there’s still room to grow, as highlighted in our ColBERT-Zero study
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcCMoNWQAA78IN.jpg
────────
[16/22] You might be worried about overfitting and so were we
So what we did is decontaminated BEIR by removing everything that overlap with our training data
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcCcdRXUAATAjn.jpg
────────
[17/22] Despite being in the toughest spot (decontamination built from our data), LateOn and DenseOn don't flinch
LateOn keeps #1, DenseOn stays top-4, only behind ColBERT-Zero (our other strong multi-vector model) and pplx-embed
That shows direct evidence of generalization and not overfitting
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGcCk2NXEAADPt2.jpg
────────
[18/22] Also, a pattern emerges: ColBERT models generalize better
All 3 ColBERT models hold or improve rank and take 2 of the top 3 spots
Dense results are more mixed, GTE-ModernBERT falls from 8th to last (although our mixture is derived from theirs, highlighting the quality of our curation). Qwen3-Embedding also drops a lot, hinting at a possible overlap with BEIR data
On the other hand, recent dense models ( jina-v5 and pplx-embed-v1) hold stronger, hinting at better generalization capabilities
────────
[19/22] We believe the models are very strong, but we also believe releasing such a large amount of data, annotations and exploration could allow a lot of new actors to come up with strong models using novel approaches
Can’t wait to see what the community will build
────────
[20/22] Collection (models/data):
Blog:
Get started with late interaction:
────────
[21/22] On a more personal note, this release is very important to me because when I started working at LightOn, two years ago, I was looking at all the top models and thinking “wow, imagine the work that it would be to achieve this”
Today, I am proud to say that with this release, LightOn put out a whole pipeline to go from totally random weights to state-of-the-art results
From ModernBERT and Ettin, to PyLate and LateOn/DenseOn, we released all the code, data and insights for anyone to go from random weights to production-ready models
And when I look back at the old me, I could not have dreamed of these resources. I am really proud of what we built and I hope it will help all the people who think that this might be too hard to do, to give it a shot and come up with their awesome models
────────
[22/22] Thanks to all the amazing people that worked on the release @raphaelsrty (my lovely co-maintainer), @orionweller (my data guy, thanks for FW!) @paulomouraj (my dearest student) and @AmelieTabatta (my boss)
Also thanks to all of the people that took part in the discussions at one point or another and gave feedback!
@xinzhangai @zach_nussbaum @tomaarsen @bo_wangbo @EYangTW @bclavie @beirmug @oskar_hallstrom @iacopo_poli

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin)
clean_title: Exploring AgentIR and BrowseComp-Plus on the Weaviate Podcast
summary:
Definitely a must watch, so excited!
BrowseComp-Plus is a very cool benchmark and AgentIR was also very interesting, I am sure the podcast is packed with information about what the future of search looks like!
I wonder what happened if we trained a late interaction model with AgentIR... guess we'll find out soon :)
Quoting @CShorten30
How do we build search systems for Agents? 👾🔎
I am SUPER EXCITED to share a new episode of the Weaviate Podcast with Zijian Chen (@zijian42chen) and Xueguang Ma (@xueguang_ma) from the University of Waterloo on AgentIR! 🎙️💚
When humans search, we write short queries and keep our reasoning in our heads. Deep Research agents do the opposite. They leave reasoning traces that reflect on prior results, clarify intent, and plan what to search next. Existing retrievers completely ignore this signal because they were designed for human queries. 💭
AgentIR jointly embeds the agent's reasoning trace alongside its query, training a retriever that actually understands what the agent is thinking. AgentIR-4B hits 68% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus compared to 52% for conventional embedding models twice its size. 📊
One idea I found especially interesting is how AgentIR raises context management questions for agents: what should be remembered, compacted, or retrieved just in time? The current reasoning trace naturally curates history by summarizing confirmed findings and filtering out wrong guesses. Forgetting becomes a feature, not a bug. 🔬
We also covered BrowseComp-Plus, their benchmark for disentangled evaluation of agents and retrievers, and the open question of scaling search deeper vs. wider.
If you're working at the intersection of Agents and Search, I think you'll get a lot out of this one! Links below! 🎉
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HG6rghAXgAEffs2.jpg
