title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin) — thread (9 tweets)
clean_title: Integrating XTR into PyLate for faster multi-vector retrieval
summary:
[1/9] XTR allows to perform multi-vector retrieval faster
But there is not much models and tooling around it, hindering its adoption
@Robro612 did a very interesting replication study and we took the opportunity to merge XTR into PyLate, alongside the awesome XTR-WARP of @hugemensa
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj6QZbWYAMs9GN.jpg
Quoting @Robro612
New 📄: we replicate XTR, a multi-vector retrieval method that makes ColBERT faster by avoiding its expensive step of gathering full document embeddings
XTR is not a free lunch over ColBERT, but its training objective is useful for modern efficient engines like PLAID and WARP 👇🏼
────────
[2/9] Train and retrieve with XTR:
Before anything, read the paper:
Usually, multi-vector goes like this
Candidates generation -> fetch/decompression of all embeddings -> full MaxSim scoring
────────
[3/9] XTR only use the first-stage candidate scores and use score imputation for the missing values, saving a lot of time by not fetching everything/skipping decompression (and not scoring everything as well)
────────
[4/9] One of the issue is that the models need to be trained to work well under these approximations
And up until today, there was not many models available, besides the original ones from Google
────────
[5/9] Today, with the merging into PyLate, you can train SOTA XTR models just by changing the score definition in your existing boilerplates
Yes, this is as easy as this
Engineering done right
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj6meuWUAAG0T4.jpg
────────
[6/9] But what would be the use of a model optimized for fast retrieval with a slow index?
Enter WARP, an index optimized for XTR retrieval
Building on the foundations of PLAID, it adds some XTR-specific optimizations to make retrieval goes brrrr
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj6wpfXEAM98Nq.jpg
────────
[7/9] Thanks to @raphaelsrty's awesome fast-plaid being open source, the awesome @hugemensa built a fork of fast-plaid to implement WARP, resulting in the excellent xtr-warp-rs library
────────
[8/9] We thus merged the WARP index into PyLate for you to easily use your new SOTA XTR models
Again, it's as simple as changing the index and retrieve type
All the API is the same!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHj7F6BXgAI-fM_.jpg
────────
[9/9] I am very much looking forward all of the insane models that will come out of this!
I want to deeply thank @Robro612 for coming up with all of the XTR code (and bearing with me during all of the tedious review cycle/shape rotating work)
Also a big thanks to @hugemensa for creating xtr-pylate-rs, very cool work (and getting better and better, sharding is insane)
And as usual, a big thanks to my dear co-maintainer @raphaelsrty for helping with all of this
clean_summary:
XTR allows for faster multi-vector retrieval, but its adoption has been limited due to a lack of models and tooling. @Robro612 conducted a replication study, leading to the integration of XTR into PyLate, along with the XTR-WARP from @hugemensa.

XTR improves efficiency by using first-stage candidate scores and score imputation, avoiding the need to fetch and decompress all embeddings. With the new integration, training state-of-the-art XTR models is simplified, requiring only a change in score definition.

The WARP index, optimized for XTR retrieval, enhances performance by building on PLAID and adding specific optimizations. The integration into PyLate allows users to easily utilize new XTR models without changing the API. This advancement is expected to lead to the development of innovative models.

title: Antoine Chaffin (@antoine_chaffin) — thread (2 tweets)
clean_title: Challenges in late interaction models for retrieval benchmarks
summary:
[1/2] Late interaction models break benches released after they were trained
But it does not mean they are perfect, far from it actually
This work is very important because it shows that our first stage retriever models are still very far from cross-encoders
Thanks for putting this out, I really think this can help getting the next generation of models and kick off new initiatives
Quoting @dianetc_
We set out to build a better retriever, so we looked for the hardest IR benchmarks.
For each, we asked how much headroom remained by running oracle reranking with a frontier LLM. Most had little room left!
So we built OBLIQ-Bench to study much harder search queries than before.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpb42wWMAcq-uC.png
────────
[2/2] The final goal of first-stage retrieval is to have a sublinear search that achieves the same performance of a cross-encoder, and to achieve that, we need to be able to take the query into account in the document representations
Despite late interaction allowing finer matching (and mogging Gemini 2 on one of the bench while being a 150M encoder 😇), it still only perform cosine similarity on a fixed embedding space. A lot of decomposed cosine, but still
I think some work like Promptriever from @orionweller would help on some of those tasks, by allowing to probe different stored "views" of the documents depending on the prompt (and thus refining a bit the search with the query), but we might need a radical paradigm shift to actually solve these tasks in general (fitting one or a few specific similarity definition would be an easy way out, but I think that's not the way we should think about those benches)
clean_summary:
Late interaction models break benchmarks released after their training, but they are not perfect. This work highlights that first-stage retriever models are still far from achieving the performance of cross-encoders. The goal of first-stage retrieval is to achieve sublinear search performance comparable to cross-encoders, which requires incorporating the query into document representations.

Despite late interaction models allowing finer matching and outperforming Gemini 2 on one benchmark while being a 150M encoder, they still rely on cosine similarity in a fixed embedding space. Exploring approaches like Promptriever could enhance search by probing different stored 'views' of documents based on the prompt, but a radical paradigm shift may be necessary to address these challenges effectively.

clean_title: Introducing Agent-ModernColBERT: Enhancing Reason-ModernColBERT's Performance
summary:
[1/13] Reason-ModernColBERT nearly solved BrowseComp-Plus, smashing SOTA and outperforming models models 54× bigger
Not bad for a 1 year old model not optimized for deep research
What if we actually tried?
Introducing Agent-ModernColBERT: adding another 10% on top with a 5 min training
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIH-OgcXsAA6wnu.jpg
────────
[2/13] Model:
Reason-ModernColBERT reached 87.56% accuracy, on BrowseComp-Plus, a 7.59 leap over previous SOTA, while toping recall AND calibration error, showing that late interaction was insanely good at agentic search
But it was not trained for agentic search
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIH9pEPXMAA9Nxi.jpg
────────
[3/13] Besides BrowseComp-Plus, @zijian42chen also created AgentIR
The idea is pretty simple: during agentic search, the agent is creating reasoning traces before generating queries
Instead of discarding those, concatenate them to the query sent to the retriever!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIH93C0WsAAgbxl.jpg
Quoting @zijian42chen
🚀 Introducing AgentIR, a retriever that reads your agent’s mind (literally!)
🧠 Unlike humans, agents explicitly expose thoughts in reasoning tokens. Put them to use!
📈 Simple, substantial gains for agents on BrowseComp-Plus, 35% (BM25) ➡️ 50% (Qwen3-Embed) ➡️ 67% (AgentIR)
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HC-zRmsXUAAIHsk.jpg
────────
[4/13] To give the capability to leverage such traces to the retriever, they generated trajectories from an agent and kindly released it as the DR-Synth dataset and trained AgentIR, a 4B dense model, outperforming larger ReasonIR-8B and pipelines with rerankers
────────
[5/13] Reason-ModernColBERT is based on ReasonIR, which is beaten by AgentIR
So you know the drill: a dense model is released alongside its data -> just feed it into PyLate and get a late interaction model that beats everything (5 min training btw)
Quoting @antoine_chaffin
By the way, when I say "lightweight" fine-tuning, I mean it
As for GTE-ModernColBERT, you can reproduce this training in less than 100 LoC and 2 hours of training
Boilerplate:
I told you there was discount on SOTA these days, come take yours with PyLate!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Grjwd5qWwAAgbgY.png
────────
[6/13] Thanks to previous explorations with Reason-ModernColBERT, we know that late interaction handles reasoning trace nicely
As expected, it performs very favorably in the AgentIR setting and enhance the already-SOTA performance by another 10% at the same cost
Quoting @antoine_chaffin
Modern retrievers can perform reasoning internally, yet they benefit from using reasoning traces from LLM!
So how does Reason-ModernColBERT perform when used in collaboration with GPT4?
Well this time it takes the crown, outperforming ReasonIR-8B and 7B rerankers!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gsr1YkVWIAA4dlQ.jpg
────────
[7/13] Notably, the setup that exposes the get_document function reaches 72.53 using GPT-OSS-120B, which is higher than the original GPT-5 + Qwen3-8B setup (that does not expose get_document, though)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIH-QmeWUAAa6lH.jpg
────────
[8/13] Agent-ModernColBERT is also very competitive with the single vector AgentIR-4B, despite being 26x smaller and trained on the same data, highlighting that late interaction is a key component for agentic search
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIH-WByXoAAYcN5.jpg
────────
[9/13] It’s important to note that, although get_document is a net improvement in most cases, the gains depends on the retrieval model and the agent being used
The very strong results of the get_document setup is thus not a given
I tried adding some other data points with the get_document function exposed, but as I was not able to reproduce the original results of AgentIR (reasonable deltas when fixing envs, but still), I do not include those in my comparison as although they seems favorable to Agent-ModernColBERT, I cannot rule out GPT-OSS related errors just yet
────────
[10/13] On the other rather interesting side notes, the model use the same prompt as AgentIR to make things comparable (up to a wrongly escaped line break!), and it seemed to have a rather limited but positive effect on the model
We’re also releasing the model trained without the prefix if that’s easier for you to use
────────
[11/13] Late interaction models are really strong for agentic retrieval, even without being trained for it
A simple lightweight training yields a model that enable a fully open-source setup competitive with GPT-5 coupled to Qwen3-8B… with a 150M model
────────
[12/13] As per usual, everything is open, the model, the data (thanks to @zijian42chen!) and the training code

Reason-ModernColBERT nearly solved BrowseComp-Plus, achieving 87.56% accuracy and outperforming models 54 times larger. This model wasn't optimized for deep research, so the introduction of Agent-ModernColBERT adds another 10% improvement with just five minutes of training.

The AgentIR model enhances agentic search by creating reasoning traces before generating queries, leading to substantial gains in performance. It outperforms larger models and pipelines, demonstrating that late interaction is crucial for agentic search. The setup also shows that modern retrievers can benefit from reasoning traces, achieving competitive results even with smaller models.

All resources, including the model, data, and training code, are open-source, allowing for easy reproduction and further exploration.

summary:

Quoting @_reachsumit
No More K-means:Single-Stage Sparse Coding for Efficient Multi-Vector Retrieval
@Veritas2026 et al. replace vector clustering with efficient sparse autoencoders & natural inverted indexing to accelerate multi-vector retrieval.
📝

clean_summary:
No More K-means introduces a method that replaces vector clustering with efficient sparse autoencoders and natural inverted indexing to speed up multi-vector retrieval. Instead of traditional clustering algorithms like K-means, this approach uses sparse coding to achieve similar or better retrieval performance with improved efficiency.

The work demonstrates that this single-stage sparse coding technique can significantly accelerate multi-vector search processes, making it more practical for large-scale applications. The linked arXiv paper provides detailed experimental results and technical insights into the method.

title: New blog post & new library are out now! The BP is about MaxSim, why it's *orders of magnitude* much more demanding than normal cosine similarity, and why — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] 📷 New blog post & new library are out now! The BP is about MaxSim, why it's *orders of magnitude* much more demanding than normal cosine similarity, and why GPUs don't care, but CPUs do! The library is maxsim-cpu, which makes it so CPUs can be fast and play it cool, too.
────────
[2/7] The links:
Github:
Blog:
────────
[3/7] Everything maxsim-cpu does is in the name: it computes MaxSim on CPU.
It's written in 🦀Rust and relies on low-level libraries
(libsxmm on x86, Apple Accelerate on Apple silicon) that can greatly speed up this sort of computations, beyond what general purpose libraries achieve.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv4qze4XgAA91P3.jpg
────────
[4/7] Note that it's specifically meant to take advantage of multiple cores and modern CPUs. If you're running it on a 4 core server, it'll probably be slower than other libs: the target is Apple Silicon (~3x speedup) and Linux servers, frequently used for retrieval inference.
────────
[5/7] The API is extremely straightforward: call maxsim cpu's two functions (one for fixed length and one for variable length documents), receive maxsim scores. Nothing more, nothing less.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv4q9rDXsAAhJ7B.jpg
────────

And if solving retrieval one piece at a time sounds like what you wanna do, we're hiring...

title: Ben Clavié (@bclavie)
summary:
This is not a major problem among us ML twitter nerds, but it's awful in enterprise settings.
Very common situation: Boss comes in, tells engs they should use the new Llama/Qwen/etc they read about on LinkedIn, it works 30% better than [whatever we were using]!
The reality: They're still using a finetuned Mistral 7B or Llama3 because there's no time on the engineering roadmap dedicated to "figuring out how to fine-tune an MoE" or "I really don't understand why Gemma is not fine-tuning properly these params used to work I swear".
Especially when historically, "just take our data and feed it to a better model" has been the norm. It's a nightmare for engineers to explain that this just doesn't work these days, because trying to use a model from a different family (or even generation, you can't FT qwen3 exactly the same way you FT'd qwen2) comes with a whole new set of issues.
Quoting @bclavie
Not to sound like a DSPy shill, but a gigantic pro of stuff like MIPRO/GEPA (cc @LakshyAAAgrawal @lateinteraction) is that it doesn't come with major suffering if you ever want to use use newer/better models.
FT/RL is fun, but upgrading your model family is exceedingly painful.

[2/9] POV: Existing training datasets are cumbersome to reproduce, requiring prerequisites such as knowledge graphs, human annotators, or paid APIs. NQ & HotpotQA contain easy questions.
> We need a frugal way to generate <hard> queries with multiple reasoning hops for search agents.

[3/9] ⚛️ORBIT construction framework — Zero prerequisites & paid APIs:
🟣 Stage 1: Seed creation via Wikipedia titles (15 domains)
🔴 Stage 2: QA-pair generation via DeepSeek Chat.
🟠 Stage 3: Self-verification via DeepSeek Chat.
🟢 Stage 4: External verification (Qwen3-4B + OSS-120B)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFOqWMObEAEF4GY.jpg
────────
[4/9] Advantages of ⚛️ORBIT framework:
1️⃣ DeepSeek Chat is publicly available with access to web search! (Zero API costs!)
2️⃣ Automation via Python Selenium — rate-limited, one prompt at a time.
3️⃣ Quality over quantity with two intensive rounds of self and external verification.
────────
[5/9] What's so good about ⚛️ORBIT?
📦 20K QA pairs across 15 domains!
🔍 Avg. 64 tokens/question, 3.5 tokens/answer!
🔗 4–6 reasoning hops needed per question!
🌐 4.36 verification URLs/pair (3.35× non-Wikipedia)!
Much more reasoning-intensive than NQ, HotpotQA, or InfoSeek!

Existing training datasets are cumbersome to reproduce, requiring prerequisites such as knowledge graphs or paid APIs. ORBIT provides a frugal way to generate hard queries with multiple reasoning hops for search agents.

ORBIT contains 20K QA pairs across 15 domains, requiring an average of 4–6 reasoning hops per question. Results show an average EM accuracy of 49.1 on Wikipedia QA datasets, significantly outperforming other models. Code and datasets are open-sourced, contributing to the research community.

clean_summary:
DFlash speculative decoding on Apple Silicon shows promising performance with Qwen3.5-9B bf16 on M5 Max. The results include 85 tokens per second at 1024 tokens with a 3.3× speedup, approximately 70 tokens per second at 1024 tokens in the video due to terminal I/O overhead, and 80 tokens per second at 2048 tokens with a 3.1× speedup.

Currently, the focus is on long context, where speedup degrades past 4K tokens due to KV cache growth, and Int4 quantized models in the 27B class. The implementation is built on MLX without CUDA on a single machine, allowing the draft to generate 16 tokens in parallel while the target verifies in one forward pass. The code will be open-sourced when ready.

The plumber came the next day, tightened a couple of nuts, and the sink worked perfectly again. The professor was delighted. But when, a minute later, the plumber handed him the bill, he was shocked.

“Yeah, I get it…” said the plumber. “Why don’t you come work for our company as a plumber? You’ll make three times more than you do as a professor. Just remember: when you apply, say you only finished seventh grade. They don’t like hiring educated people.”
So the professor got a job as a plumber, and his life really did improve. All he had to do was tighten a nut here and there every so often, and his salary was much higher.
One day, the management of the plumbing company decided that every plumber had to attend evening classes to finish eighth grade. So our professor had to go too.
By chance, the very first class was math.
The evening school teacher, wanting to check what the students knew, asked for the formula for the area of a circle.
They called the professor up to the board, and he suddenly realized he’d forgotten it. He started frantically reasoning it out, covering the board with integrals, differentials, and all sorts of fancy formulas to re-derive the result. In the end, he got:
S = –π r²
He didn’t like the minus sign, so he started again.
Again he got a minus. No matter what he did, it kept coming out negative.
He cast a panicked look at the class, and all the plumbers were whispering:
“Swap the limits of integration!”

title: @burkov
clean_title: Classifier-free guidance for text-to-image diffusion models
summary:
Generating an image from a sentence used to require a separate classifier trained on noisy images just to steer the output toward the prompt.
This paper from OpenAI shows you can drop that. The core idea is classifier-free guidance: during training the text caption is sometimes replaced with an empty one, so a single model learns to predict image noise both with and without text; at generation time you take the difference between the text-conditioned and unconditioned predictions and exaggerate it, which sharpens how closely the image follows the caption with no extra classifier.
The authors built a 3.5 billion parameter diffusion model around this, and human evaluators preferred its output to DALL-E (OpenAI's then-main system at twelve billion parameters) about 87% of the time for photorealism, even when DALL-E was allowed to generate many candidates and keep the best; they also finetuned the same model to fill erased image regions from a prompt, with matching shadows and reflections, making text-driven editing practical.
Classifier-free guidance went on to become standard and is still used in the systems leading the field in 2026 (FLUX.2, later Stable Diffusion, the models behind DALL-E 3 and Imagen).

clean_title: From code generation to AI agents: the evolving role of code in long-running systems
summary:
LLMs have moved from producing standalone code to powering AI agents — systems that plan over many steps, call external tools, keep track of changing state, and recover from their own errors during long-running tasks.
Inside these systems, code has become the working material for almost everything: agents write small programs to reason through math, to drive a browser, to query a database, to test their own outputs, and to share intermediate work with other agents through files in a repository.
Existing surveys still treat code mainly as the final answer that a model produces. The authors of this paper argue this misses the broader role code now plays inside agent systems.
They use the term "agent harness" for the scaffolding around a model (planning, memory, tool calls, and execution-based verification loops) that turns one-shot generation into something that can run for hours on a real task, and they organize their map of this scaffolding into three connected layers: the interface, covering how code lets an agent reason, act, and represent its environment; the mechanisms, covering how planning, memory, tool use, and feedback-driven repair keep long executions on track; and the scaling layer, covering how several agents share repositories, tests, and execution traces to coordinate.
Each layer is tied to concrete systems such as Claude Code and Codex, and to application areas including software engineering, GUI and OS automation, embodied robots, scientific discovery, and personalization.

great thread between @lateinteraction and @Teknium
anyone working with long context should read it.
RLMs are fascinating.
Quoting @lateinteraction
The following are not standard in a coding agent:
1. The user prompt P itself (not just external data) is a symbolic object in the environment. The model is not allowed to grep/read long snippets from P.
2. The model has to write recursive code (that calls LMs) to understand or transform the content of P. Unlike "sub-agents", recursion must happen during code execution, which means that you can launch arbitrarily many sub-calls, not just a small constant number, without polluting the context window.
3. All sub-calls and tool calls return values into symbolic variables. The model is not allowed to pollute its context window with their return values. Instead, it must build up (and refine) its output with recursion.
Contrast Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 to see the formal differences.

title: Cameron R. Wolfe, Ph.D. (@cwolferesearch)
clean_title: Confidence calibration techniques for neural networks and large language models
summary:
I wrote an overview of confidence calibration techniques a while ago:
It was one of the earliest posts on my newsletter and was inspired by work in grad school. Models / techniques have changed a lot, but I think the learnings are transferable.
Quoting @cwolferesearch
As LLMs have gained more autonomy, recent research has focused more on measuring the reliability of models / systems (e.g., Pass^K metrics or surfacing problems to users). Calibration (one of my personal favorite research areas) is one of the most useful concepts for measuring and improving reliability.
Intuitively, calibration measures whether the model is confident only when it is right. Practically, we can measure calibration using the probabilities (e.g., token probabilities from an LLM) outputted by a model, which can be interpreted as a confidence score. Ideally, the probability of a prediction should be perfectly correlated with the likelihood of accuracy. For example, if we have P(output) = 0.5, then the probability of this output being correct should be 50%.
Unfortunately, this is not the case for most modern neural networks. The structure of the cross entropy objective incentivizes over-confidence. We optimize the training objective by maximizing the probability of correct predictions. As a result, all predictions tend to be made with very high confidence whether they are correct or not.
To measure whether our model is calibrated, we can use metrics like Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Given a set of predictions each with a corresponding confidence score, we compute ECE by separating predictions into bins based on their confidence score and examining accuracy within each bin:
ECE = \sum_{m=1}^M (|B_m| / N) * |acc(B_m) - conf(B_m)|
where M is the number of bins, B_m is the set of examples in bin m, N is the total number of examples, and acc / conf are the accuracy and confidence score within a bin.
Confidence calibration is an entire area of research with a long history that studies the problem of improving the calibration of neural networks. As a starting point, I would recommend reading this paper:
This is one of my all-time favorite papers, and I’m really excited to see how similar ideas can be applied to building more reliable systems with the impressive foundation models we have today.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIOV_rCW0AAGFgm.jpg
clean_summary: Confidence calibration measures whether a model's confidence scores accurately reflect its likelihood of being correct. For example, if a model outputs a probability of 0.5, it should be correct about 50% of the time. Many modern neural networks tend to be overconfident due to the training objective, which maximizes the probability of correct predictions. Calibration metrics like Expected Calibration Error (ECE) evaluate how well confidence scores align with actual accuracy by grouping predictions into confidence bins and comparing accuracy within each. Improving calibration is an active research area, with foundational work available in papers such as 'On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks' and 'Confidence Calibration for Deep Networks,' which aim to make neural network confidence scores more meaningful and reliable.

I'm wrapping up a writeup on how to evaluate agents. The overview uses Terminal-Bench and Tau-Bench as the primary case studies, but I'm including the following benchmarks as well:
- GAIA and GAIA-2 ( general assistant benchmarks that require reasoning, web browsing, tool use, and handling multimodal data.
- AgentCompany ( knowledge work benchmark that uses agents to simulate a small software company by browsing information, writing code, and talking with each other to complete tasks.
- WorkArena ( knowledge work benchmark that evaluates the ability of agents to solve enterprise software workflows sourced from ServiceNow.
- OSWorld ( computer-use benchmark that tests the ability of agents to solve common tasks in real desktop environments. Various other computer-use benchmarks like OfficeBench and MobileBench exist as well.
- MLE-Bench ( autonomous experimentation benchmark that tests whether agents can solve machine learning problems from Kaggle. Other machine learning agent benchmarks like PostTrainBench and MLGym also exist.
- PaperBench ( machine learning benchmark that tests the ability of agents to reproduce AI research papers from arxiv.
- SpreadsheetBench ( excel-based benchmark that test the ability of agents to perform various types of spreadsheet manipulations.
- HIL-Bench ( human-in-the-loop benchmark that evaluates whether agents can decide when to ask humans to clarify ambiguous task specifications.
- GDPval ( realistic benchmark that tests the ability of agents to solve various types of economically-valuable tasks.
What am I missing? Please send me more benchmarks!!

pgGraph is built around the idea that Postgres should remain the source of truth while the graph engine operates alongside it. It keeps the rows in Postgres, compiles the topology around them, and creates a virtual graph layer using CSR-style adjacency arrays. This approach allows existing Postgres databases to be graph-traversable for agents without the usual complications, such as recursive join issues, ETL pipelines, or maintaining a second source of truth, all while ensuring blazing fast performance.

pgGraph is already live in production workflows across various sectors, including RevOps, healthcare, and visa services. clean_title: Three mechanisms causing oblique queries in information retrieval
summary:
We identify three mechanisms through which queries become "oblique", where relevance is latent and has little surface expression in the document.
With these, we build five hard IR tasks where even first-stage search is a bottleneck.
Each breaks retrieval in a different way👇

title: Diane (@dianetc_) — thread (4 tweets)
clean_title: Testing seven IR systems including GPT-5.2 and Oracle Tournament
summary:
[1/4] We test seven IR systems, from the state-of-the-art dense models and late interaction models to search agents, where GPT-5.2 searches, reads, notes, and repeats for a few rounds.
We compare these against Oracle Tournament, which sets a fuzzy upper bound on our tasks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpcTDrWYAEQLpk.png
────────
[2/4] Descriptive queries target latent properties without naming them. Twitter-Conflict asks for tweets that imply a specific stance through framing or irony, with explicit/news tweets as hard distractors. WildChat Errors finds model failures that are never explicitly mentioned.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpcapGW0AMN52Y.png
────────
[3/4] Analogue queries seek documents with the same abstract structure but different surface content. Math Meta-Program retrieves problems solved by the same proof strategy across fields and Writing-Style finds posts by the same author across a multitude of topics.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpcfTbXYAUiLwM.png
────────
[4/4] Oblique tip-of-tongue queries match a fuzzy, lossy recollection to one obscure passage.
Congress Hearings: "Someone sent me this clip where a senator starts off weirdly friendly, then flips and starts pinning the guy down…"
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpcjt6X0AEneHN.png
clean_summary:
We test seven information retrieval systems, ranging from state-of-the-art dense models and late interaction models to search agents like GPT-5.2, which searches, reads, notes, and repeats for a few rounds. These systems are compared against Oracle Tournament, which sets a fuzzy upper bound on our tasks.

Descriptive queries target latent properties without naming them, such as Twitter-Conflict, which asks for tweets implying a specific stance through framing or irony, and WildChat Errors, which identifies model failures that are never explicitly mentioned.

Analogue queries seek documents with the same abstract structure but different surface content, like Math Meta-Program, which retrieves problems solved by the same proof strategy across fields, and Writing-Style, which finds posts by the same author across various topics.

Oblique tip-of-tongue queries match fuzzy recollections to obscure passages, exemplified by Congress Hearings, where a user recalls a clip of a senator starting off friendly before turning confrontational.

title: Diane (@dianetc_)
clean_title: OBLIQ-Bench highlights gaps in retrieval architectures for reasoning LLMs
summary:
Across all 5 tasks, reasoning LLMs can verify relevance once they see the document, but lexical/dense/agentic retrievers struggle to surface it. Several surprising lessons!👇
We hope OBLIQ-Bench helps identify what retrieval architectures still miss and how to close that gap.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHpcpCcXgAEQPPs.png
clean_summary:
Across all five tasks, reasoning LLMs can verify relevance once they see the document, but lexical, dense, and agentic retrievers struggle to surface it. Several surprising lessons emerge from this.

We hope OBLIQ-Bench helps identify what retrieval architectures still miss and how to close that gap.

title: François Chollet (@fchollet)
clean_title: Misconceptions about scalability in AI methods
summary:
There's a broadly held misconception in AI that methods that scale well are simple methods -- even, that simple methods usually scale. This is completely wrong.
Pretty much none of the truly simple methods in ML scale well. SVM, kNN, random forests are some of the simplest methods out there, and they don't scale at all. Meanwhile "train a transformer via backprop and gradient descent" is a very high-entropy method, easily 10x more complex than random forest fitting. But it scales very well.
Further, given a simple method that doesn't scale, it is usually the case that you alter it to make it scale by adding a lot of complication. For instance, take a simple a simple combinatorial search-based method (not scalable at all) -- you can make it scale by adding deep learning guidance (which blows up complexity). Scalability usually belongs to high-entropy, complex systems.
clean_summary:
There's a broadly held misconception in AI that methods that scale well are simple methods, and that simple methods usually scale. This is completely wrong. Pretty much none of the truly simple methods in machine learning, like SVM, kNN, and random forests, scale well. Meanwhile, training a transformer via backpropagation and gradient descent is a very high-entropy method, easily ten times more complex than fitting a random forest, yet it scales very well.

Furthermore, when you have a simple method that doesn't scale, it is usually altered to make it scalable by adding a lot of complication. For example, a simple combinatorial search-based method (which is not scalable at all) can be made to scale by incorporating deep learning guidance, which significantly increases complexity. Scalability typically belongs to high-entropy, complex systems.

title: Femke Plantinga (@femke_plantinga)
summary:
Should you fine-tune your embedding model?
(Spoiler: probably not 𝘺𝘦𝘵)
𝘉𝘦𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦 jumping into fine-tuning, ask yourself: is your retrieval pipeline actually failing because of domain-specific knowledge gaps, or could it be something simpler?
Here's what to check first:
• Are you using the right chunking technique? Maybe late chunking would help
• Do you need exact keyword matches? Try hybrid search instead
• Is your current model just not capturing enough contextual nuances? A model with more dimensions might solve this
𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻-𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽𝘀, 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲-𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗶𝘁.
Fine-tuning embedding models works differently than fine-tuning LLMs. Instead of next-token prediction, it uses contrastive learning methods that adjust vector distances in embedding space.
The core principle: given an anchor data point, which candidate is most similar? The optimization process pulls positive pairs closer together while pushing negative pairs apart.
Popular loss functions include:
→ 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗡𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝗥𝗮𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗼𝘀𝘀: Simple text pairs, treats other batch examples as negatives
→ 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘁 𝗟𝗼𝘀𝘀: Requires careful curation of (anchor, positive, negative) triplets
→ 𝗖𝗼𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗼𝘀𝘀: Uses similarity scores for graded relationships
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗻𝗲𝘄𝘀? Fine-tuning costs way less than pre-training - sometimes just a few dollars for simple tasks, and you can even run smaller models on Google Colab's free tier.
𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀: Start with 1,000-5,000 high-quality samples for narrow domains, scale to 10,000+ for complex specialized terminology.
Once you've fine-tuned a model and pushed it to @huggingface, you can use it directly with @weaviate_io through either the Hugging Face integration or AWS SageMaker.
But remember - fine-tuning should be your last resort, not your first instinct. Often, the solution is simpler than you think.

🔍🪡To find the needle, you better index every straw of the haystack.
Today, LightOn is launching LightOn NextPlaid: a CPU-optimized multi-vector database that indexes at the token level. By representing documents as sets of vectors, one per token, we preserve the distinct concepts and precise details that other search engines average away.
Why NextPlaid is the missing layer for your RAG stack:
🎯Precision Matching: Retrieval matches at the token level, surfacing the exact passage that answers your question rather than just a document that vaguely relates.
📉Frugal Inference: High-signal context reduces the amount of noise sent to your LLM, allowing it to answer with fewer, more accurate tokens.
🚀Seamless Integration: NextPlaid runs alongside your existing vector database. You can add multi-vector retrieval to your established RAG pipeline without ripping anything out.
⚙️Production Ready: Built in Rust and optimized for CPUs, it supports incremental index updates and concurrent reads/writes—capabilities missing from standard implementations.
NextPlaid represents the "Blanc" milestone in our Bleu/Blanc/Rouge roadmap for enterprise document intelligence. It follows the "Bleu" release, LightOnOCR-2, a SOTA 1B OCR model which converts complex documents into clean, usable text.
Huge kudos to @raphaelsrty for shipping this breakthrough! 🙌

At Nvidia we're really into synthetic data and how to make better agents, faster. I was really excited about this technique from @DongfuJiang , @zhuofengli96475 and team and I wanted to reproduce their SDG in Data Designer with our new release. Check it out!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA6qr7tasAAdpCP.jpg
Quoting @DongfuJiang
🚀 Introducing OpenResearcher: a fully offline pipeline for synthesizing 100+ turn deep-research trajectories—no search/scrape APIs, no rate limits, no nondeterminism.
💡 We use GPT-OSS-120B + a local retriever + a 10T-token corpus to generate long-horizon tool-use traces (search → open → find) that look like real browsing, but are free + reproducible.
📈 The payoff: SFT on these trajectories turns Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B from 20.8% → 54.8% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus (+34.0).
🧩 What makes it work?
🔎 Offline corpus = 15M FineWeb docs + 10K “gold” passages (bootstrapped once)
🧰 Explicit browsing primitives = better evidence-finding than “retrieve-and-read”
🎯 Reject sampling = keep only successful long-horizon traces
🧵 And we’re releasing everything:
✅ code + search engine + corpus recipe
✅ 96K-ish trajectories + eval logs
✅ trained models + live demo

clean_summary:
S3 is the perfect place to store data until you try to search it. I built Firn, an open-source, multi-tenant vector and full-text search engine on S3, inspired by turbopuffer. It combines foyer (RAM/NVMe cache), LanceDB (S3-native storage), and an axum REST API.

With 100,000 vectors, the performance results show that searching in cold S3 takes 25.1 seconds, while using the warm cache reduces this to just 72 microseconds, achieving a 350,000x speedup.

The linked GitHub project details the cost efficiency of S3 with the speed of local RAM, featuring a tiered architecture for microsecond latency on top of object storage.

title: Leonie (@helloiamleonie)
summary:
Multi-vector embeddings (e.g., ColBERT) are powerful but expensive to scale.
MUVERA cuts their memory costs by 70%.
MUVERA (Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings) is an interesting approach by Google Research. It transforms multi-vector representations into single fixed-size vectors (fixed dimensional encodings).
MUVERA uses a 4-step process:
1. Space partitioning (using k-means or LSH)
2. Dimensionality reduction via linear projections
3. Multiple repetitions for accuracy
4. Final projection
MUVERA works well in our experiments (LoTTE dataset tests):
• Memory footprint reduced by ~70%
• Import time reduced by ~70-85%
• HNSW graph size: Reduced by ~99%
Yes, there's some loss in recall quality. But you can mitigate this by increasing the HNSW ef parameter value during search.
Learn more about MUVERA, how it performed in our experiments, and whether it might be worth exploring for your use case:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G5KE-wNXQAA2cuG.png

title: Leonie (@helloiamleonie)
summary:
Scaling agent memory across thousands of tenants?
Flat index support with rotational quantization landed in @weaviate_io 1.34.
It’s ideal for multi-tenancy scenarios with many small tenants, where brute-force search with quantization is fast enough without the memory overhead of HNSW graphs.
We already know vector quantization is cool because it reduces the memory footprint of vector embeddings. Less storage, lower costs, faster vector search.
Cool, cool, cool.
But what’s so special about rotational quantization?
In simplified terms:
Think of rotational quantization like scalar or binary quantization, but with an added rotation step.
This rotation process turns vectors with ill-suited distributions into well-suited ones:
Ill-suited:
Mixture of large and small entries
→ wide quantization interval → less precision
Well-suited:
smoothed and tightly concentrated around zero
→ short quantization interval → higher precision
That means a well-suited distribution allows you to capture more subtle differences between values than an ill-suited one.
And this leads to lower quantization error.
Learn more about rotational quantization here:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G6DHpNWWYAA4W6I.png

summary:
[1/10] Very excited to release WARP!
Coded in Rust 🦀 and with Python bindings, WARP is currently the fastest engine for multi-vector search, being close to 10x faster than the current SOTA (FastPlaid) 🚀
Details and benchmarks below 👇
────────
[2/10]
────────
[3/10] While WARP was initially designed for XTR variants, it also works out of the box with any late interaction model trained with a maxsim objective, including ColBERT, ColPali, and many others!
────────
[4/10] I benchmarked WARP across 8 datasets using a non-XTR model.
On a 5090, the average improvement in QPS (queries per second) is 755%, ranging from 326% on Quora to 982% on FiQA.
────────
[5/10] On a CPU (AMD 9950X) the improvement is even more dramatic.
Using 32 threads, QPS improvements jump to an average of 3806%, ranging from 1243% on TREC-COVID to 7106% on NFCorpus.
Single-threaded performance averages 1311%, ranging from 431% on TREC-COVID to 2654% on SciFact.
────────
[6/10] In fact, almost all benchmarked datasets (6 out of 8) running on 32 threads beat the current SOTA on CUDA by 1.5-3x!
────────
[7/10] Despite the amazing search performance, the engine has a lot of room to grow: Retrieval metrics are a bit worse (2% drop on average), index creation is 10x slower and memory usage is 20% higher.
Still, the repo is under active development and contributions are welcome!
────────
[8/10] The code is based on the WARP paper by @jlscheerer, @matei_zaharia, @ChrisGPotts, @lateinteraction (et al.)
It deviates a bit from the source material by adding some improvements to default parameter selection, long query handling and in the decompression and merging stages.
────────
[9/10] The WARP library sits on top of other amazing software.
FastKMeans for centroid computation, by @bclavie, a lot of boilerplate code from FastPlaid, by @raphaelsrty, and tch-rs, which exposes the C++ PyTorch API to Rust.

title: Pau (@hugemensa) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Finally released v1.0.0 of WARP 🦀
This version adds mutability to the index, meaning you can now add, update and delete documents from the index without having to recreate it
Researching this led me to some interesting empirical findings unique to WARP, details below 👇
────────
[2/8] After each addition, the engine checks for outlier embeddings. If enough are found, it expands the centroids, keeping cluster quality stable as the distribution shifts. The outlier detection threshold is recalibrated via a weighted average so it adapts to the evolving data
────────
[3/8] I benchmarked this across 5 BEIR datasets, by creating partial indices with a subset of the full data and then adding the rest of the documents
Findings show that batching documents for big updates result in almost no degradation at all, both in retrieval metrics and in QPS 🚀
────────
[4/8] "Streaming" docs instead of batching the updates shows an increase in retrieval metrics but a decrease in QPS. This makes sense, since the centroid expansion is triggered more often, ending up with more centroids (higher recall/ndcg, but index is denser, which tanks QPS)
────────
[5/8] Despite all that, WARP is not immune to the bad init problem: you need >3k docs OR >50% of the distribution upfront for good centroids. Otherwise, retrieval metrics degrade 10-20% as the index grows
────────
[6/8] This is exclusively a WARP weakness that I could not reproduce in PLAID. Both use centroids for IVF candidate lists, but PLAID fully decompresses docs so its dependency ends there. WARP still relies on centroids for missing score estimation
────────
[7/8] This release was fun, with many small optimizations: distances from compacted residuals, O(1) delete, no doc ID rolling, auto-compaction at a deletion threshold, etc. The defaults ensure consistent results but the package remains easy to use and tunable ⚡️
────────
[8/8] As always kudos to @raphaelsrty, your code is an amazing baseline. And @antoine_chaffin I can finally start drafting the PR for pylate, since I can now fit WARP to the exposed protocol

clean_summary:
WARP v1.1.3 has been released, adding metadata filtering to the engine. The exposed API remains the same as FastPlaid's, but internal changes have been made to boost performance.

WARP now uses DuckDB and PyArrow instead of SQLite, making filtering operations 10-20 times faster. This change allows the package to natively support all DuckDB types and operations, providing a powerful interface.

Filtering is performed using a boolean lookup table, implemented through a bitset in CPU for O(1) performance and a tensor of booleans in CUDA for O(n) performance, which grows with index size. This will likely be the last release for WARP, aside from bug fixes and feature requests, as new ideas for future developments are already in mind.

title: Han Xiao (@hxiao)
summary:
What if we force an embedding model to generate text? how would that look like? Well, I tried it, and results are pretty interesting. I flattened the jina-embeddings-vv4 retrieval LoRA back to its Qwen2.5-VL base and asked v4 to generate as an LLM.
The output looks like gibberish at first but also kinda makes sense: repeating the original tokens, sub-tokens, synonyms in diff. languages, then repeat repeat repeat. It does remind me of that ICLR 2025 paper by @jacspringer "Repetition Improves Language Model Embeddings," which trains embeddings using an LLM by simply duplicating the input to counter the autoregressive effect.
So that paper's "echo embeddings" hack flips the autoregressive curse—where early tokens miss future context—by repeating the sequence so the second half gets full bidirectional vibes through the model's attention. In my experiment, we're seeing the inverse: v4 spits out these loops of repeats and synonyms, generating "augmentations" that keep semantic similarity maxed out. So there, repetition fixes gen models for embeddings; here, repetition exposes how embedding models "generate" by echoing their contrastive roots.
Wild what it hints—maybe there's another way to train embeddings, less like infoNCE, more like how we train LLM today?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gv87hk0XYAAJF2B.png

title: Han Xiao (@hxiao) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] after turboquant and qwen3.5-35b-a3b, i got curious: how realistic is it to use kv cache as a document store today? to have vectorless, RAG-less search. so i prefilled 258K out of 262K context window on L4 (a budget GPU popular in prod). ~99% of the slot is pre-computed and stored, users load it on the fly in ~1s. system prompt + query append to the end, generation takes ~3K tokens, enough for search. at 99% fill rate, decoding runs ~20 tps on L4.
i prepared some ego datasets (jina papers, which i know best), plus popular novels in chinese and english. the results are actually pretty good. some hallucination, but most answers are solid and well-grounded. what's more interesting is the cost: ~$0.26/h on L4 spot. single LLM. no vector database, no embedding model, no workflow/pipeline engineering.
using kv cache as document store is nothing new, like the old CAG paper. but with quantized kv cache and modern attention (hybrid SSM-attention, GQA, MQA, MLA), the economics are changing fast. if we solve cold-prefill speed and decoding speed, and budget GPU costs keep dropping, the future of search could be vectorless. radical, but possible.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2038292074777174016/img/dRJbAFNPfIjuCnXf.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2038292074777174016/vid/avc1/320x424/QsbkYzKRN4tCHyIC.mp4?tag=21
────────
[2/2] KV cache can be a way of embedding knowledge. on L4 for 258K tokens, it takes 572s to embed, much slower than any embedding model we have. but once embedded, every query runs against full attention over the entire document. no chunking loss, no retrieval miss. recall is theoretically perfect - you're attending to everything. try the demo here:
the obvious ceiling is the context length: 262K tokens is roughly one book. to scale to 10 books or an enterprise KB, you'd need multi-slot routing - pick the right embedded slot per query.
finally, i still found the latest upstream llama.cpp cannot reliably handle prefilled cache reuse at long context (>200K) for qwen-3.5-35b-a3b. i know i've been back and forth on this multiple times, sending alarms and then false alarms. anyway, i made my PR here, which is essential to make the demo work:

title: Isaac Flath (@isaac_flath) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] Q: Why is semantic search for code coming back? (Cursor, mgrep, etc)
A: Multi-vector architecture
Q: Why do I care?
MUCH less token usage + better responses if used
Q: What makes it work?
A: Token (not chunk) level embeddings with extreme quantization
Here's what I learned 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyBblbgAAls2d.jpg
────────
[2/9] mgrep (by @mixedbreadai) is how I've been using this. It works with any coding agent as a CLI tool.
More embeddings (token vs chunk) means more info, which makes sense. But how can that scale?
It comes down to the quantization
Here's the core ideas:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyCXJa0AAfQxP.jpg
────────
[3/9] In the simplest form, quantization is a bit like rounding numbers. You give up precision to save space.
With scalar quantization, instead of storing a full 64-bit number, you can store an 8-bit code representing its approximate value (8x compression ratio).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyDQtaIAEu7rP.jpg
────────
[4/9] Step 1: Split each embedding in half (make sub-vectors).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyFEFbgAcmH0d.jpg
────────
[5/9] Step 2: Cluster each collection of sub-vectors separately to find the centroids
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyF8MbgAYKyT-.jpg
────────
[6/9] Step 3: Store which cluster/centroid each piece belongs to
Step 4: reconstruct by looking up centroids and combining
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyGx1bsAAuRz5.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyG7RbgAUbpgb.jpg
────────
[7/9] Step 5: Extreme Quantization
ColBERT goes one step further. After PQ, it calculates the "residual" error (the small difference between the original and the approximation). Then, it quantizes that error, often down to just 1 or 2 bits per value!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G7GyHydaMAAx0Gp.jpg
────────
[8/9] This two-stage compression (PQ + residual quant) means you get token-level understanding in fraction of the space

Talk 2:

title: Jo Kristian Bergum (@jobergum)
summary:
Many of you know me as the bm25 guy but I'm afraid there is no single silver bullet for solving retrieval for agents. You also need to make the data retrievable in the first place.
Yes, agents are great at formulating queries and they are relentless so classic issues like vocabulary missmatch are arguably less of a concern when the agent is doing the queries. But, a lot of the context that we would like to feed agents with it isn't represented in text so embeddings are still very important to cover more modalities. Making more data useful.
We now see the early raise of multi-modal embeddings handling a mix of modalities into the same embedding space which I'm directionally excited about.
For example, there is a lot of talk about the context layer for enterprises and especially here multimodal representations is key. Think meeting nodes, audio, images (e.g images of pdf pages).
So even if I'm the bm25 guy, I still think embeddings will play a big role in the context layer for agents.

clean_title: Open sourcing Witchcraft: a local search engine from Dropbox
summary:
[1/4] Open sourcing something fun from @Dropbox: Witchcraft.
It's a local search engine built in Rust with no API keys or vector DB required.
Think: ColBERT / late interaction style retrieval, but packaged to run locally (perfect for coding agents).
Let's dive in👇
────────
[2/4] Under the hood, it's a from-scratch implementation of XTR-WARP, a retrieval approach in the ColBERT family.
So instead of collapsing everything into one embedding, it keeps the richer multi-vector / late interaction setup that tends to preserve meaning better.
────────
[3/4] It also supports hybrid retrieval.
That means you can combine:
- lexical search / BM25
- semantic search
- late interaction scoring
Which, in practice, is often the right answer. Semantic or grep is rarely enough.
────────
[4/4] The repo even includes Pickbrain, an example that indexes Claude Code and OpenAI Codex session transcripts, memory files, and authored docs into a Witchcraft database for fast search.
Context quality = coding quality
clean_summary:
Open sourcing something fun from @Dropbox: Witchcraft. It's a local search engine built in Rust with no API keys or vector database required. Think of it as ColBERT/late interaction style retrieval, but packaged to run locally, making it perfect for coding agents.

Under the hood, it's a from-scratch implementation of XTR-WARP, a retrieval approach in the ColBERT family. Instead of collapsing everything into one embedding, it maintains a richer multi-vector/late interaction setup that tends to preserve meaning better.

Witchcraft also supports hybrid retrieval, allowing you to combine lexical search/BM25, semantic search, and late interaction scoring. In practice, this combination is often the best solution, as semantic or grep alone is rarely sufficient.

The repository even includes Pickbrain, an example that indexes Claude Code and OpenAI Codex session transcripts, memory files, and authored documents into a Witchcraft database for fast search. The quality of context correlates with coding quality.

title: Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy)
summary:
Agency > Intelligence
I had this intuitively wrong for decades, I think due to a pervasive cultural veneration of intelligence, various entertainment/media, obsession with IQ etc. Agency is significantly more powerful and significantly more scarce. Are you hiring for agency? Are we educating for agency? Are you acting as if you had 10X agency?
Grok explanation is ~close:
“Agency, as a personality trait, refers to an individual's capacity to take initiative, make decisions, and exert control over their actions and environment. It’s about being proactive rather than reactive—someone with high agency doesn’t just let life happen to them; they shape it. Think of it as a blend of self-efficacy, determination, and a sense of ownership over one’s path.
People with strong agency tend to set goals and pursue them with confidence, even in the face of obstacles. They’re the type to say, “I’ll figure it out,” and then actually do it. On the flip side, someone low in agency might feel more like a passenger in their own life, waiting for external forces—like luck, other people, or circumstances—to dictate what happens next.
It’s not quite the same as assertiveness or ambition, though it can overlap. Agency is quieter, more internal—it’s the belief that you *can* act, paired with the will to follow through. Psychologists often tie it to concepts like locus of control: high-agency folks lean toward an internal locus, feeling they steer their fate, while low-agency folks might lean external, seeing life as something that happens *to* them.”
Quoting @garrytan
Intelligence is on tap now so agency is even more important

title: Andrej Karpathy (@karpathy)
summary:
Don't think of LLMs as entities but as simulators. For example, when exploring a topic, don't ask:
"What do you think about xyz"?
There is no "you". Next time try:
"What would be a good group of people to explore xyz? What would they say?"
The LLM can channel/simulate many perspectives but it hasn't "thought about" xyz for a while and over time and formed its own opinions in the way we're used to. If you force it via the use of "you", it will give you something by adopting a personality embedding vector implied by the statistics of its finetuning data and then simulate that. It's fine to do, but there is a lot less mystique to it than I find people naively attribute to "asking an AI".

I packaged up the "autoresearch" project into a new self-contained minimal repo if people would like to play over the weekend. It's basically nanochat LLM training core stripped down to a single-GPU, one file version of ~630 lines of code, then:
- the human iterates on the prompt (.md)
- the AI agent iterates on the training code (.py)
The goal is to engineer your agents to make the fastest research progress indefinitely and without any of your own involvement. In the image, every dot is a complete LLM training run that lasts exactly 5 minutes. The agent works in an autonomous loop on a git feature branch and accumulates git commits to the training script as it finds better settings (of lower validation loss by the end) of the neural network architecture, the optimizer, all the hyperparameters, etc. You can imagine comparing the research progress of different prompts, different agents, etc.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary: I'm just going to start tweeting my research hot takes. I think they're very actionable and they'll help you assess and produce AI research much better than implicit conventional wisdom in many cases.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
DSPy's biggest strength is also the reason it can admittedly be hard to wrap your head around it.
It's basically say: LLMs & their methods will continue to improve but not equally in every axis, so:
- What's the smallest set of fundamental abstractions that allow you to build downstream AI software that is "future-proof" and rides the tide of progress?
- Equivalently, what are the right algorithmic problems that researchers should focus on to enable as much progress as possible for AI software?
But this is necessarily complex, in the sense that the answer has to be composed of a few things, not one concept only. (Though if you had to understand one concept only, the fundamental glue is DSPy Signatures.)
It's actually only a handful of bets, though, not too many. I've been tweeting them non-stop since late 2022, but I've never collected them in one place.
All of these have proven beyond a doubt to have been the right bets so far for 2.5 years, and I think they'll stay the right bets for the next 3 years at least.
1) Information Flow is the single most key aspect of good AI software.
As foundation models improve, the bottleneck becomes basically whether you can actually (1) ask them the right question and (2) provide them with all the necessary context to address it.
Since 2022, DSPy addressed this in two directions: (i) free-form control flow ("Compound AI Systems" / LM programs) and (ii) Signatures.
Prompts have been a massive distraction here, with people thinking they need to find the magical keyword to talk to LLMs. From 2022, DSPy put the focus on *Signatures* (back then called Templates) which force you to break down LM interactions into *structured and named* input fields and *structured and named output fields*.
Getting simply those fields right was (and has been) a lot more important than "engineering" the "right prompt". That's the point of Signatures. (We know it's hard for people to force them to define their signatures so carefully, but if you can't do that, your system is going to be bad.)
2) Interactions with LLMs should be Functional and Structured.
Again, prompts are bad. People are misled from their chat interaction with LLMs to think that LLMs should take "strings", hence the magical status of "prompts".
But actually, you should define a functional contract. What are the things you will give to the function? What is the function supposed to do with them? What is it then supposed to give you back?
This is again Signatures. It's (i) structured *inputs*, (ii) structured *outputs*, and (iii) instructions. You've got to decouple these three things, which until DSP (2022) and really until very recently with mainstream structured outputs, were just meshed together into "prompts".
This bears repeating: your programmatic LLM interactions need to be functions, not strings. Why? Because there are many concerns that are actually not part of the LLM behavior that you'd otherwise need to handle ad-hoc when working with strings:
- How do you format the *inputs* to your LLM into a string?
- How do you separate *instructions* and *inputs* (data)?
- How do you *specify* the output format (string) that your LLM should produce so you can parse it?
- How do you layer on top of this the inference strategy, like CoT or ReAct, without entirely rewriting your prompt?
Signatures solve this. They ask you to *just* specify the input fields, output fields, and task instruction. The rest are the job of Modules and Optimizers, which instantiate Signatures.
3) Inference Strategies should be Polymorphic Modules.
This sounds scary but the point is that all the cool general-purpose prompting techniques or inference-scaling strategies should be Modules, like the layers in DNN frameworks like PyTorch.
Modules are generic functions, which in this case take *any* Signature, and instantiate *its* behavior generically into a well-defined strategy.
This means that we can talk about "CoT" or "ReAct" without actually committing at all to the specific task (Signature) you want to apply them to. This is a huge deal, which again only exists in DSPy.
One key thing that Modules do is that they define *parameters*. What part(s) of the Module are fixed and which parts can be learned?
For example, in CoT, the specific string that asks the model to think step by step could be learned. Or the few-shot examples of thinking step by step should be learnable. In ReAct, demonstrations of good trajectories should be learnable.
4) Specification of your AI software behavior should be decoupled from learning paradigms.
Before DSPy, every time a new ML paradigm came by, we re-wrote our AI software. Oh, we moved from LSTMs to Transformers? Or we moved from fine-tuning BERT to ICL with GPT-3? Entirely new system.
DSPy says: if you write signatures and instantiate Modules, the Modules actually know exactly what about them can be optimized: the LM underneath, the instructions in the prompt, the demonstrations, etc.
The learning paradigms (RL, prompt optimization, program transformations that respect the signature) should be layered on top, with the same frontend / language for expressing the programmatic behavior.
This means that the *same programs* you wrote in 2023 in DSPy can now be optimized with dspy.GRPO, the way they could be optimized with dspy.MIPROv2, the way they were optimized with dspy.BootstrapFS before that.
The second half of this piece is Downstream Alignment or compile-time scaling. Basically, no matter how good LLMs get, they might not perfectly align with your downstream task, especially when your information flow requires multiple modules and multiple LLM interactions.
You need to "compile" towards a metric "late", i.e. after the system is fully defined, no matter how RLHF'ed your models are.
5) Natural Language Optimization is a powerful paradigm of learning.
We've said this for years, like with the BetterTogether optimizer paper, but you need both *fine-tuning* and *coarse-tuning* at a higher level in natural language.
The analogy I use all the time is riding a bike: it's very hard to learn to ride a bike without practice (fine-tuning), but it's extremely inefficient to learn *avoiding to ride the bike on the side walk* from rewards, you want to understand and learn this rule in natural language to adhere ASAP.
This is the source of DSPy's focus on prompt optimizers as a foundational piece here; it's often far superior in sample efficiency to doing policy gradient RL if your problem has the right information flow structure.
That's it. That's the set of core bets DSPy has made since 2022/2023 until today. Compiling Declarative AI Functions into LM Calls, with Signatures, Modules, and Optimizers.
1) Information Flow is the single most key aspect of good AI software.
2) Interactions with LLMs should be Functional and Structured.
3) Inference Strategies should be Polymorphic Modules.
4) Specification of your AI software behavior should be decoupled from learning paradigms.
5) Natural Language Optimization is a powerful paradigm of learning.
Quoting @DSPyOSS

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
Isn't the solution here obvious? Does one need to write a paper to make this point?
RLHF needs an upgrade: Ask experts to look at LLM trajectories and offer not pointwise/pairwise bits, but:
- written feedback
- targeted edits
Then work on learning algorithms (definitely not GRPO!) that can learn from this detailed feedback. You already have some like dspy.GEPA or dspy.SIMBA.
But it's easy to imagine a much larger space of these. This massively increases the "bits per FLOP" and still keeps all the trial-and-error and "task focus" of RL.
Quoting @dwarkesh_sp
Interesting post. Bits/FLOP from RL are 3-6 OOMs lower than pretraining.
Though @tamaybes made the point that the bits from RL can target the specific skills you want to learn. Whereas pretraining just distributes those bits over learning random ASCII relationships and a million other irrelevant things.
Furthermore, for any given task, there's lots of decisions whose specific execution doesn't matter much, and a couple you really want to nail. RL can concentrate the signal towards learning how to not mess up the critical states in the episode, as opposed to getting every single token correct. Useful image from one of @svlevine's old lectures (B is the critical state):
I think this still nets out to RL being far far less information dense than pretraining. And I agree with Toby that intelligence gain per FLOP of RL env training will be less than many assume.
Working on a post about this with @EgeErdil2, @MatthewJBar, and @tamaybes. Hopefully we can publish next week.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
Your periodic reminder that late interaction isn’t “awesome but takes a lot of space” as I see here often.
ColBERT vectors are often 10 bytes each. Ten bytes. That’s like 3-4 floats.
It’s about *interactions* (aka ~attention) not “many vectors”.
It’s not “many vectors work better than one vector”. It’s “set similarity works better and trains better than a rigid dot product”.
Even with the same storage cost! You can’t fix this by making one vector bigger. You don’t need a lot of storage of the mini-vectors for late interaction.
It’s just that dot products suck.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
This may sound like some kind of unusual argument, but it’s the same reason you use a Transformer and not an LSTM.
Your representations don’t need to be crammed into a vector, scalable kNN similarity doesn’t need to be a dot product. And this shift doesn’t need to be expensive.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
On RLMs: The way people tend to implement recursive sub-calls or “sub-agents” don’t work.
In particular, you cannot express sub-agents as tool calls.
To see why those aren’t expressive enough, suppose you are given a 10M-token prompt that starts with “keep each math question below iff the answer is an even number”.
A typical sub-agent strategy would fail on a few angles:
1) It can’t *write* the O(N) sub-calls as tool calls, because the model can’t verbalize that many explicit sub-prompts. In other words, the recursion has to be symbolic through code, not tool calls.
2) It also can’t fit the long prompt in the first place—so it may resort to compaction. In other words, it’s crucial for an RLM that its own prompts/requests (not just the typical external “environment”) are accessible through pointers as an object, so it can recurse through them symbolically.
Just wanted to note these because I see people get excited then implement ideas that are much less expressive than RLMs are supposed to be.

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
New updates for the RLM paper:
We post-trained RLM-Qwen3-8B at tiny scale, the first natively recursive LM.
And it's pretty promising, even on completely unseen types of tasks! We just released the model too.
Some quick thoughts here:
Training a model to be good at long-context processing is known to be really hard. How can such a tiny model learn to be a decent RLM in general, from very little data?
We think part of the answer is that RLMs are extremely modular.
To learn to be a root RLM, the model doesn't need subtle changes to how it uses attention or something. It just needs to recognize the programmatic format of interacting with prompts-as-variables and to bake in good strategies for writing little recursive programs.
That's... not even as tricky as post-training models for solving hard math problems.
Once the sub-calls are launched, they're ~pretty much normal LLM calls, so no special training is particularly necessary (though we're sure it might help).
Obviously, this is just meant as a simple PoC that shows that tiny models can be good RLMs.
We call on future work to train native RLMs at much larger scales in terms of model size, number and variety of examples, and number of (ideally on-policy and online!) rollouts.
Quoting @a1zhang
We just updated the RLM paper with some new stuff.
First, we just released RLM-Qwen3-8B, the first natively recursive language model (at tiny scale!).
We post-trained Qwen3-8B using only ~1000 RLM trajectories from unrelated domains to our evaluation benchmarks.
RLM-Qwen3-8B works well across several tasks and delivers a pretty large boost over using an RLM scaffold with the underlying Qwen3-8B model off-the-shelf, and even larger gains over directly using Qwen3-8B directly for long-context problems.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_2MiqOWAAAgPlB.png

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
The following are not standard in a coding agent:
1. The user prompt P itself (not just external data) is a symbolic object in the environment. The model is not allowed to grep/read long snippets from P.
2. The model has to write recursive code (that calls LMs) to understand or transform the content of P. Unlike "sub-agents", recursion must happen during code execution, which means that you can launch arbitrarily many sub-calls, not just a small constant number, without polluting the context window.
3. All sub-calls and tool calls return values into symbolic variables. The model is not allowed to pollute its context window with their return values. Instead, it must build up (and refine) its output with recursion.
Contrast Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 to see the formal differences.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HAk-72CXAAAn4ya.png

title: Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction)
summary:
The size of the representation is not very important. You can always increase the dimension of a single-vector embedding. It barely helps.
The important thing is interaction: different pieces in the query can attend to (or align with) different pieces in the document.
This modularity makes learning good representations much more generalizable. It's very easy to learn a representation of a primitive concept (or a keyword).
It's extraordinarily hard to learn a single vector such that a dot product captures deep relationships across distributions of queries and documents.
Because of this, the size of late-interaction (multi-vector) representations of a passage is often *much smaller* than off-the-shelf single-vector representations you get from using float16 to encode a 4096-dimensional vector. Each vector in late interaction encodes extremely compact information, often representable with as little as 20 bytes.
Quoting @nickinpractice
@softwaredoug @lateinteraction Thanks! From a first read it seems the main benefit is the "effective" query embedding size grows linearly with the input, since you're not compressing the query into a single vector but into one vector per query token. So it's more expressive.

🚨Typical RL algorithms and on-policy distillation methods are blind samplers: they use privileged info to score rollouts, but not to *find* them.

Latent Terms: Dense Retrievers Contain Trivially Extractable BM25-ready Zipfian Vocabularies

clean_summary:
Omar Khattab is very excited to share a new work that is very topical now. A blog post about it is coming soon.

The linked arXiv paper introduces a method where dense retrievers contain trivially extractable, BM25-ready Zipfian vocabularies. The work shows how sparse features that are indexable and compatible with traditional information retrieval metrics can be reconstructed from frozen dense retrievers using reconstruction-trained sparse autoencoders.

transpose alone is very fast because it simply creates a view of the existing data with different shape and stride information, just changing how pytorch interprets the memory layout without moving any actual data around, making it an O(1) constant time operation. when you add contiguous(), pytorch is forced to physically reorganize and copy all the tensor data in memory to make it laid out sequentially according to the new dimensions, which becomes an expensive O(n) operation that scales with tensor size.

title: @matospiso
summary:
I’ll close this opinion-piece by saying that even though I pointed out an aspect of the eval that I’m not satisfied with, I still believe the results are overall convincing and the model seems strong.
Research is complex.
For a final takeaway, let’s pretend for a minute this whole discussion is about knives, not embeddings.
Knives are used for numerous tasks but probably most commonly for cooking - and so there’s a huge market for versatile kitchen knives: chef’s knives. It only makes sense that many consumer comparisons test knives on kitchen prep work - cutting bread, dicing onions, fileting fish, you name it.
However, there’s another major group of customers buying knives whose needs require something way more precise than a chef’s knife. Surgeons use scalpels - probably because performing a surgery with a chef’s knife is a bad idea. To choose which scalpel to buy, I assume the procurement team in a hospital would be interested in the scalpel’s performance on, e.g., a cataract surgery task.
Back to embedding models.
Single-vector models are like chef’s knives - if you need one model to cover all your needs, they are probably your best bet.
BM25 is like a scalpel - it’s much more precise but less versatile. For example, it’s not clear how to extend it to modalities other than text.
Multi-vector representations are like a hypothetical combination of the two - versatile like single-vector but with much higher precision thanks to the rich MaxSim scoring operator.
⭐️ Here’s, in my view, the main point of the release: @mixedbreadai’s new model demonstrates that it is possible to achieve both versatility and surgical precision in a single model; they forged the combined knife type with very strong performance on a whole bunch of tasks.
The results are undeniably impressive and they will inspire others to try out multi-vector representations.
But outperforming just chef’s knives on a cataract surgery benchmark will not impress eye surgeons.
That’s all.
(8/8)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDU9safbwAAuWNY.jpg

summary:
We are currently working on quantization-aware training to speed up retrieval. My colleagues have published a blog post about first results - more is on the way!
Quoting @JinaAI_
Cliché is that quantization hurts performance—that you must trade quality for space. Reality? Skill issue. Learn how we trained quantized versions of jina-embeddings-v4 using Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), where models learn to work with rounding rather than fight against it. QAT integrates quantization constraints directly into training, allowing models to adapt and compensate for quantization effects. This includes Low-Rank QAT (LR-QAT), which reduces weight and activation redundancy, and efficient frameworks like EfQAT that optimize training to achieve near-full precision accuracy with lower computational overhead.

title: Mihir Prabhudesai (@mihirp98)
summary:
We ran more experiments to better understand “why” diffusion models do better in data-constrained settings than autoregressive. Our findings support the hypothesis that diffusion models benefit from learning over multiple token orderings, which contributes to their robustness and reduced overfitting.
To test this, we trained autoregressive (AR) models with varying numbers of token orderings: N=1 corresponds to the standard left-to-right ordering, while N=k includes the left-to-right order plus k−1 additional random permutations. As N increases, we observe that AR models become more data-efficient, exhibiting improved validation loss and reduced overfitting.
All models were trained for 100 epochs, and were evaluated using the standard left-to-right factorization. We also experimented with related approaches, such as RAR and σ-GPT, and observed consistent trends --introducing more random factorizations led to better generalization and less overfitting.
We have updated our arXiv submission with these new results. We thank @giffmana and @YouJiacheng for suggesting these experiments.
Original paper post -
