title: Sigrid Jin 🌈🙏 (@realsigridjin)
clean_title: LightOn's LateOn and DenseOn retrievers for improved retrieval performance
summary:
@LightOnIO one of the last hope for ir community
i still believe retrieval is not dead, it has potential beyond mere markdown mgmt for agentic memories
they opensourced two retrievers, LateOn and DenseOn
both 149M params, apache 2.0, trained on identical data with different architectures
the interesting finding is what happens when you actually test generalization
dense retrieval = squash each doc into one vector at index time, compare against query vector
fast, but lossy, you're throwing away everything you didn't compress
late interaction (colbert-style) = keep a vector per token. match token-to-token at query time
more compute, way more information preserved
beir is the standard benchmark
problem: training corpora overlap with eval corpora, so scores measure familiarity as much as retrieval quality
so lighton rebuilt the eval. stripped every document from beir that appeared in their training data
dense models dropped in rank under decontamination. colbert models held or climbed. average delta was +2.01 for dense, +3.55 for multi-vector
so your corpora are niche, internal, domain-specific, the model has never seen them
that's exactly the regime where compressed dense vectors fall apart and late interaction keeps working

The new generation of open state-of-the-art single and multi-vector retrieval models is here

title: Rudy Gilman (@rgilman33)
summary:
DINO-v3 has a single high-magnitude channel on its residual pathway, channel 416. Turning off this single channel affects DINO's entire output by 50-80%. For context, turning off a random channel has an effect of less than one percent.
The model builds up channel 416 in its last two layer-scale operations, using a single high-magnitude weight in each op to drastically ramp up channel 416's magnitude. This channel doesn't depend on the input, every image fires with a constant overlay.
After bringing channel 416 up to a value of about ten thousand, DINO-v3 then scales it down in the final layer-norm to almost nothing, removing it without a trace.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1959976785506160640/img/ox4GpfGCdALd89HR.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1959976785506160640/vid/avc1/480x270/63Zfk3uZvZ75RrDO.mp4?tag=21

title: Simon Willison (@simonw)
clean_title: LiteParse: An open-source PDF document parser using heuristics
summary:
LiteParse is really neat! It does a great job of extracting text from annoying layouts in PDFs (multiple columns for example)
It's only available as a Node.js CLI app, so I vibe-coded up this version that runs in a browser
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGnzE6HbIAA1mA8.jpg
Quoting @jerryjliu0
LiteParse, our OSS document parser, is really good at parsing complex PDF layouts, text, and tables into a clean spatial grid.
The best part is it doesn't use VLMs or any ML models at all. It's entirely heuristics based and super fast ⚡️
The secret lies in our sophisticated grid projection algorithm. This blog post by @LoganMarkewich gives a comprehensive walkthrough on how it works:
1️⃣ Sort lines based on similar Y coordinates
2️⃣ Extract left, right, and center anchors
3️⃣ Classify every text item into one of these anchors
4️⃣ Project every text item into a grid column (the exception is any paragraph of flowing text, which is rendered separately)
5️⃣ For any item projected into a grid column, that item is the forward anchor for all subsequent text items with the same anchor
6️⃣ Postprocess the final outputs to remove extraneous spaces and margins
As an example, take a look at the results below. You can see text in the left column, with a nicely overlaid table on the right.
LiteParse is fully free and open-source, you can use it today! Either directly through the CLI or integrated into your coding agent.
Blog:
LiteParse repo:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGiM2qQa0AA57Ww.jpg

title: Doug Turnbull (@softwaredoug)
summary:
Search teams can learn from this late interaction win of @LightOnIO and @antoine_chaffin
Late interaction uses fewer parameters more efficiently than a direct cross encoder. It lets you remember a document / query's representation for reuse for future searches.
It's easy to get hung up on "oh but it generates an embedding per token" - but the alternative of a full transformer model with parameters that interact query / document at every layer is much more burdensome / slow.
I expect we'll *finally* begin to see widespread deployment of late interaction models this year - especially as agentic use cases ramp up.

summary:
[1/12] 📷 You might have seen a lot of OCR release recently... Here is another one, introducing 🦉 LightOnOCR-1B A fully end-to-end differentiable VLM model competing with all the latest releases while being much faster🚀
────────
[2/12] 2/10
blog:
Most OCR systems rely on complex multi-stage pipelines
🦉 LightOnOCR-1B replaces them with a single fully differentiable model.
It handles structured layouts such as tables, forms, and equations directly, without brittle preprocessing steps
────────
[3/12] 3/10
Quality (Olmo-Bench)
• Outperforms DeepSeekOCR
• Matches dots.ocr (~3× larger)
• +16 points vs Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct
• No benchmark-specific fine-tuning
LightOnOCR-1B achieves state-of-the-art performance in its weight class.
────────
[4/12] 4/10
Efficiency
Single H100 GPU (80 GB):
• 5.71 pages / s ≈ 493 000 pages / day
• 6.49× faster than dots.ocr
• 2.67× faster than PaddleOCR-VL-0.9B
• 1.73× faster than DeepSeekOCR
• < $0.01 per 1 000 pages
A compact model that’s both high-quality and cost-efficient.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G39GhPlW8AAKiKv.jpg
────────
[5/12] 5/10
Training
Distilled from Qwen2-VL-72B-Instruct using a curated corpus of 17.6 M pages and 45.5 B tokens
All rendered from PDFs at native resolution and normalized into Markdown — lightweight, token-efficient, and semantically consistent.
Dataset to be released openly.
────────
[6/12] 6/10
Ablations & Findings
• Single-stage > two-stage (+1.4 avg)
• Larger teacher (72B vs 7B) → +11.8 pts
• Vocabulary pruning (→ 32 k) preserves accuracy + improves speed
• Fine-tuning (+9 pts in 1 epoch on OlmOCR-mix)
────────
[7/12] 7/10
Vocabulary pruning
Reducing Qwen3’s vocab 151 k → 32 k / 16 k tokens:
• Maintains English/French accuracy
• ≈ 12 % faster decoding
• Expected loss on non-Latin scripts
Shows how domain-specific tokenization can improve OCR efficiency.
────────
[8/12] 8/10
Architecture
A native-resolution ViT (Pixtral-based) connects to a Qwen3 language model through a compact multimodal projection layer.
Documents rendered at 200 DPI (max 1540 px).
Higher inference resolution → +6 pts on dense text and math pages.
────────
[9/12] 9/10
Finetuning and Adaptability
End-to-end trainability makes specialization straightforward.
On OlmOCR-mix (doc subset):
• +9 pts overall after 1 epoch
• +51 pts on headers & footers
Surpasses MonkeyOCR-3B and approaches MinerU 2.5 performance with minimal effort.
────────
[10/12] 10/10
Summary
🦉 LightOnOCR-1B
• 1 B params | End-to-end | Fast | Open data
• SOTA quality / cost balance
• Easy to serve with vLLM
Available models:

[11/12] LightOnOCR-1B was developed with awesome colleagues @baptaubertin and @CavaillesAdrien at @LightOnIO !

[1/11] 📷 🚀 LightOnOCR-2-1B 🦉 is out, a major update to LightOnOCR. 1B parameters, end-to-end multilingual OCR, and it beats models 9× larger on OlmOCR-Bench while being much faster. PDF/page in, clean ordered Markdown out, with optional image localization (bbox variants).
────────
[2/11] SoTA performance at 1B scale. LightOnOCR-2-1B scores 83.2 ± 0.9 on OlmOCR-Bench, with standout gains on ArXiv, old scans with math, and tables.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_CzbkoXgAAyRrf.png
────────
[3/11] What changed vs the original LightOnOCR?
A 2.5× larger and cleaner training mix (better scans, French, scientific PDFs), improved data curation and higher-resolution training.
The best part is the data is open source on @huggingface
────────
[4/11] Speed matters 🏎️
⚡ Speed: 5.71 pages/s on a single H100 80GB (vLLM). That’s 3.36× faster than Chandra and 6.49× faster than dots.ocr.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_C0qNPXgAACZJP.png
────────
[5/11] We push quality further with RLVR inspired by the excellent work on OlmOCR-2 by @allen_ai!
We add extra rewards for KaTeX rendering/formatting and add compression-based rewards to penalize looping behaviors.
This reduces repetitions by more than 50% and pushes OCR to a new SOTA
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_C1--QWEAAIori.png
────────
[6/11] How well does it perform on image localization in documents?
It matches 9B baselines in terms of raw IoU and exceeds them in F1 and count accuracy!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_C4h6RW4AERmHz.png
────────
[7/11] Here’s one example from @AmelieTabatta’s PhD notes 🦉📄
Want more? Check the @huggingface Space to explore outputs interactively. You can zoom into the page and hover the input image to compare.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G_C870eXQAE4JGT.jpg
────────
[8/11] Try it on your own documents in the live demo 🦉
────────
[9/11] Collection (model weights, datasets, benchmark):
Blog post:
────────
[10/11] preprint with all the technical details is coming soon!
────────
[11/11] LightOnOCR-2-1B is a team effort with @CavaillesAdrien and @baptaubertin at @LightOnIO 🦉🚀

title: Thomas Fel (@thomas_fel_) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Thrilled to share that our work investigating recurrence in trained ViTs has been accepted at #ICLR2026! 🎉
It turns out DINOv2 may be secretly recurrent.🦖
A 2-block recurrent transformer can match its activations layer-by-layer and recover 96% of its ImageNet performance.
🧵
Quoting @mozesjacobs
Are ViTs secretly RNNs? #ICLR2026
Our 2-block recurrent transformer recovers 96% of DINOv2’s IN-1k accuracy & reproduces its activations 1-to-1, motivating the Block-Recurrent Hypothesis:
w/ @thomas_fel_ @RichieHakim @ABrondetta Demba Ba @t_andy_keller
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/HAvVexyWkAALNPr.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/HAvVexyWkAALNPr.mp4
────────
[2/3] Implication 1: If the Block-Recurrent Hypothesis holds, it means these networks have remarkably low Kolmogorov complexity — and arguably low Levin complexity too, since the recurrent program is not just short but fast to execute.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA0FEwua4AAkHYW.jpg
────────
[3/3] Implication 2: If ViTs are effectively recurrent, we could study them using dynamical systems tools. That's exactly what we propose — and we find that tokens converge into class-dependent angular attractors, with trajectories that self-correct after perturbation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HA0Ff_mXUAA4jI5.jpg

title: @tomaarsen — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] We're announcing a new update to MTEB: RTEB
It's a new multilingual text embedding retrieval benchmark with private (!) datasets, to ensure that we measure true generalization and avoid (accidental) overfitting.
Details in our blogpost below 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2L2OoQW8AAXJMn.jpg
────────
[2/5] Read our full blogpost:
🧵
────────
[3/5] In short: RTEB uses a hybrid approach with both open and private datasets to measure generalization, preventing overfitting to test sets.
The picture at the top of this thread is what we commonly see on MTEB: models with lower zero-shot score higher, but generalize worse.
🧵
────────
[4/5] With RTEB, we can see the differences between public and private benchmarks, displayed in this figure here.
This would be an indication of whether the model is capable of generalizing nicely.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2L2zEiWQAAWjdU.jpg
────────
[5/5] The benchmark is multilingual (20 languages) and covers various domains (general, legal, healthcare, code, etc.), and it's already available on MTEB right now.
There's also an English only version available.

title: @tomaarsen — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] 🔥I've just published Sentence Transformers v5.2.0!
It introduces multi-processing for CrossEncoder (rerankers), multilingual NanoBEIR evaluators, similarity score outputs in mine_hard_negatives, Transformers v5 support and more.
Details in 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G75UGjzWsAA9Wih.jpg
────────
[2/8] CrossEncoder multi-processing:
Similar to SentenceTransformer and SparseEncoder, you can now use multi-processing with CrossEncoder rerankers. Useful for multi-GPU and CPU settings, and simple to configure:
just `device=["cuda:0", "cuda:1"]` or `device=["cpu"]*4` on the `model.predict` or `model.rank` calls.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G75SiF-XwAAkkKH.jpg
────────
[3/8] Multilingual NanoBEIR Support:
You can now use community translations of the tiny NanoBEIR retrieval benchmark instead of only the English one, by passing `dataset_id`, e.g. `dataset_id="lightonai/NanoBEIR-de"` for the German benchmark.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G75Q3ZxWIAESWo4.jpg
────────
[4/8] Similarity scores in Hard Negatives Mining:
When mining for hard negatives to create a strong training dataset, you can now pass `output_scores=True` to get similarity scores returned. This can be useful for some distillation losses!
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G75RPC3XwAAvid2.jpg
────────
[5/8] Transformers v5:
This release works with both Transformers v4 and the upcoming v5. In the future, Sentence Transformers will only work with Transformers v5, but not yet!
Even my tests run on both Transformers v4 and v5.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G75RYh1XMAAkOjc.png
────────
[6/8] Python 3.9 deprecation:
Now that Python 3.9 has lost security support, Sentence Transformers no longer supports it.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G75RdpoXkAIhT2B.png
────────
[7/8] Check out the full changelog for more details:
And don't forget to ⭐ the project if you haven't yet.
🧵
────────
[8/8] I'm quite excited about what's coming. There's a huge draft PR with a notable refactor in the works that should bring some exciting support. Specifically, better multimodality, rerankers, and perhaps some late interaction in the future!

clean_title: Sentence Transformers v5.4: Fully multimodal embeddings and reranking
summary:
[1/9] 🌐 I've just released Sentence Transformers v5.4: we're going fully multimodal for embeddings & reranking!
Also featuring a modular CrossEncoder, and automatic Flash Attention 2 input flattening.
Highlights in 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFd78WeWQAAn74U.png
────────
[2/9] I wrote a blog post walking through the new multimodal capabilities with practical examples. Check it out if you want to get started, or just point your Agent to the URL:
🧵
────────
[3/9] SentenceTransformer now natively supports text, images, audio, and video (or combinations). Encode any modality with the same .encode() API, then compare across modalities with .similarity().
Works out of the box with models like Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFd8EVzW8AIE0cN.jpg
────────
[4/9] What if you want to combine fully separate encoders for different modalities? The updated Router module lets you do exactly that: route inputs to the right encoder based on detected modality.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFd8LZvXIAANamv.jpg
────────
[5/9] CrossEncoder also goes multimodal. Rerank text documents against an image query (or any combination of modalities).
Models like jinaai/jina-reranker-m0 work out of the box.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFd8PcUWsAANHQ3.jpg
────────
[6/9] CrossEncoder is now fully modular, i.e. a torch.nn.Sequential of composable modules, just like SentenceTransformer.
This unlocked generative rerankers (CausalLM-based) via a new LogitScore module. Models like mxbai-rerank-v2 and Qwen3 rerankers now work without custom code.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFd8SlpWQAA-JRz.jpg
────────
[7/9] Flash Attention 2 now automatically skips padding for text-only inputs. All sequences are concatenated into a single flat tensor - no wasted compute on padding tokens.
The gains grow with input length variance. Free speedup + lower VRAM.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HFd8Vs0XsAAw15K.png
────────
[8/9] This release has set up the groundwork for more easily introducing late-interaction models (both text-only and multimodal) into Sentence Transformers in the next major release. Looking forward to it!
pip install sentence-transformers[image,audio,video]==5.4.0
🧵
────────
[9/9] Full release notes with a lot more details:
clean_summary:
I've just released Sentence Transformers v5.4, which goes fully multimodal for embeddings and reranking. It features a modular CrossEncoder and automatic Flash Attention 2 input flattening.

I wrote a blog post walking through the new multimodal capabilities with practical examples. SentenceTransformer now supports text, images, audio, and video natively, allowing encoding of any modality with the same .encode() API and comparison across modalities with .similarity(). The updated Router module lets you combine separate encoders for different modalities.

The CrossEncoder can now rerank text documents against an image query, and it is fully modular, enabling generative rerankers via a new LogitScore module. Flash Attention 2 automatically skips padding for text-only inputs, optimizing compute efficiency. This release lays the groundwork for introducing late-interaction models in the next major update.

clean_title: Improving first-stage relevance in text search with non-text attributes
summary:
BM25 efficiently scores text, but relevance often depends on more than text (recency, popularity, PageRank)
we score non-text attributes as clauses in the same MAXSCORE plan that evaluates BM25 → better first-stage relevance, still scales to 100M+
clean_summary:
BM25 efficiently scores text, but relevance often depends on more than just text, such as recency, popularity, and PageRank. We score non-text attributes as clauses in the same MAXSCORE plan that evaluates BM25, leading to better first-stage relevance while still scaling to over 100 million items.

The linked article explains how turbopuffer now allows combining attribute values into the scoring function of text queries, helping achieve better relevance in the first stage with the same scalability characteristics as BM25.

clean_title: Faster filtered counts on TPU with bitmap operations
summary:
filtered counts on tpuf just got much faster
our ANN index may replicate docs across clusters for better recall, so we had to dedupe matching IDs (slow)
now, we store a bitmap of replica positions so the query plan is pure bitmap ops:
(filter_bitmap - replica_bitmap).popcnt()

clean_summary: Filtered counts on TPU just got much faster. Our ANN index may replicate documents across clusters for better recall, so we had to deduplicate matching IDs, which was slow. Now, we store a bitmap of replica positions, allowing the query plan to consist of pure bitmap operations: (filter_bitmap - replica_bitmap).popcnt().

title: Victoria Slocum (@victorialslocum)
summary:
Looking for a cheaper, open source alternative to agentic RAG?
Try multi-vector retrieval with Reason-ModernColBERT.
Most search systems compare one big summary vector per document. Multi-vector retrieval is different - it keeps separate vectors for each word or phrase, then finds the best matches between your search and the document pieces.
Reason-ModernColBERT is a small but mighty model trained on the reasonir-hq dataset and specializes in finding documents that require logical thinking, not just keyword matching.
It actually outperforms models 45x larger on reasoning tasks with just 150M parameters - tiny compared to billion-parameter models. It also creates small 128-dimension vectors and handles documents up to 8,000+ words long.
So while agentic RAG uses LLMs to tackle complex questions requiring intricate planning, multi-step reasoning, and utilization of external tools, sometimes you don't need all that complexity. Multi-vector retrieval gives you smart search results at a fraction of the cost.
Ready to try it? Check out this notebook by @helloiamleonie:

title: Xin Eric Wang (hiring postdoc) (@xwang_lk)
clean_title: Xin Eric Wang (hiring postdoc) on data gating and reward grounding in self-play RL
summary:
This is a very important finding for self-play RL. I really like the distinction between the data gate and the reward — what enters the training loop and how it is optimized are two different levers.
The finding that upstream data gating can be the binding constraint for stability feels especially important for understanding self-play and self-improving systems.
This also resonates with our recent work on verifiable environment construction for stable self-improvement. Excited to see more discussion around this direction.
EvoEnv:
Quoting @xwang_lk
We discover the 𝐀𝐬𝐲𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜 𝐑𝐨𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐆𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐟-𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐲 𝐑𝐋: data gating, not reward grounding, is the binding constraint on stability. A strict gate stabilizes every reward we tested, including a self-consistency reward with no access to ground truth; while no reward stabilizes once the gate is removed, not even one grounded in execution truth.
It challenges the common assumption that reward grounding is what governs self-play stability. The field's response to collapse has been better rewards: confidence penalties, momentum anchors, hacking detectors, all on the reward side. The binding constraint lives upstream, in the data pipeline.
A self-play system has two distinct levers that prior work conflates. A DATA GATE decides which proposer-generated tasks enter the training pool. A REWARD decides how the policy updates on what's admitted. The gate decides what data exists; the reward decides how the optimizer reacts. They are not symmetric!
The reward doesn't filter bad data; instead, it's maximized by it. Under self-consistency, the intrinsic–grounded gap saturates near 1.0: corrupted data receives higher reward than clean data, because intra-group agreement is easiest to maximize on ambiguous tasks.
The counterintuitive consequence we call the Grounded Proposer Paradox: a proposer with ground-truth verification access collapses FASTER than an ungrounded one when paired with a self-consistency solver. Cleaner tasks form the lowest-resistance path to the spurious self-consistent attractor. The upstream agent doesn't bias the downstream one toward truth; it sharpens the corridor to the wrong fixed point.
The shift: stop treating self-play stability as a reward-design problem. What enters the training loop matters more than how the optimizer scores it.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI8BK_zbsAAD6bz.jpg
clean_summary: This finding highlights that in self-play reinforcement learning, the upstream data gating process, which controls what data enters training, is a key factor for system stability, rather than the reward signal itself. A strict data gate stabilizes training even without access to ground truth rewards, challenging the common assumption that reward grounding governs stability. Instead, the data pipeline upstream acts as the binding constraint, with a self-play system having two separate levers: the data gate and the reward. The data gate determines which tasks are included, while the reward influences how the policy updates on those tasks. Experiments show that corrupted data can receive higher rewards than clean data under self-consistency, leading to the Grounded Proposer Paradox, where an agent with ground-truth access collapses faster than an ungrounded one. The key insight is that focusing on what data enters training is more important for stability than reward design.

title: Yuntian Deng (@yuntiandeng)
clean_title: Direct Corpus Interaction for agentic search without embedding models or vector indices
summary:
🚀 Introducing DCI-Agent — Direct Corpus Interaction for agentic search.
No embedding model. No vector index. No retrieval API. Just terminal-style operations like grep, read, bash, regex, and lightweight scripts to directly operate over large-scale local corpora.
Result: higher accuracy with lower token cost.
I have been thinking a lot about what retrieval should look like when agents become stronger at planning, coding, and tool use. Classic RAG and retrieval agents expose a corpus through a top-k retriever: efficient, scalable, and extremely useful — but also a compressed interface. The agent only sees what the retriever decides to surface.
A simple analogy: top-k retrieval is like asking a librarian to bring you a small cart of likely relevant books. DCI is closer to an open-stack research library, where the agent can enter the corpus, search exact phrases, inspect nearby context, follow weak clues, and verify hypotheses locally.
For humans, walking through the library would be painfully slow. For agents and computers, grep, file reads, and small scripts make this kind of direct interaction cheap, composable, and surprisingly effective.
This is the core question we wanted to study:
As foundation models become stronger, is top-k retrieval still the best interface for search — or is it becoming a bottleneck?
📈 The results are surprisingly strong.
On BrowseComp-Plus, with the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 backbone:
🔎 Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever: 69.0% accuracy, $1,440
🧰 DCI-Agent-CC: 80.0% accuracy, $1,016
That is +11.0 accuracy points while reducing cost by 29.4%.
DCI also generalizes beyond deep research, reaching 83.0 avg accuracy on multi-hop QA and 68.5 avg NDCG@10 on IR ranking — without relying on conventional sparse/dense retrieval pipelines.
🧩 The most interesting finding is why DCI works.
DCI does not simply win by retrieving more gold documents. In many cases, retrieval agents already surface useful evidence, but fail to convert it into the next reasoning step.
It helps because it gives the agent higher retrieval interface resolution. Once the agent reaches a promising document, it can localize, inspect, compose, and verify evidence at a much finer granularity.
The gain is less about “more recall” and more about turning weak evidence into actionable evidence.
That said, DCI is not a free lunch.
Our ablations show a clear operating envelope: DCI is powerful once it finds a useful anchor document, but as the corpus grows, finding that first anchor becomes more expensive. In short, DCI scales well in search depth, but not automatically in search breadth.
The tool-set and context-management results point to the same lesson. A simple read + grep interface already captures much of the gain, while open bash improves accuracy further at higher cost. And for long-horizon search, the best context strategy is not to keep the most text, but to preserve the right working state.
So the takeaway is not: “Replace every retriever with grep.” The stronger point is that retrieval for agents should become an interface-design problem, not only a retriever-design problem.
I believe future retrieval agents will be hybrid and adaptive: semantic retrieval to find anchors, DCI-style interaction to inspect and verify evidence, and context management to keep long searches stable.
The question is no longer only:
“Which embedding model gives the best top-k?”
It is also:
“What operations should an agent have over knowledge?”
DCI is our first step toward this direction: treating retrieval as a high-resolution interaction layer between agents and corpora.

#LLM #AgenticSearch #Retrieval #RAG #Agents #DeepResearch #InformationRetrieval #ToolUse

🚀 We replaced the entire agentic search pipeline — embedding model, vector index, top-k retrieval — with only `grep` and `bash`. 🔧
📄 Paper:
DCI unlocks the full agentic potential of any Claude Sonnet 4.6: 69.0% → 80.0% on BrowseComp-Plus (+11.0, −$424).
💡The Magic:
The agent searches the raw corpus directly — `grep`, `find`, `bash`, shell pipelines — exactly like a coding agent navigating a codebase. No preprocess. No embedding model. No vector index. No offline indexing.
📊The Results:
DCI outperforms top baselines across 13 benchmarks, with average gains of:
🔍 Agentic Search: +11.0%
🧠 Multi-hop QA: +30.7%
📈 IR Ranking: +21.5%
💡 Insights:

DCI-Agent introduces a new approach to search for agents by directly interacting with large-scale local corpora using terminal-style operations like grep, read, bash, and regex, instead of relying on embedding models, vector indices, or retrieval APIs. This method achieves higher accuracy at lower token costs and offers a finer retrieval interface, allowing agents to inspect, localize, and verify evidence more effectively.

The results show that DCI outperforms traditional top-k retrieval methods, with an 11-point accuracy increase on BrowseComp-Plus while reducing costs by nearly 30%. It also generalizes well to multi-hop QA and IR ranking tasks. The key insight is that improving the retrieval interface resolution, rather than just increasing recall, enables more effective reasoning and evidence utilization. Future retrieval systems for agents are likely to be hybrid, combining semantic anchors with direct, script-based interactions and sophisticated context management.
